articles.title: Quanti sono davvero i femminicidi in Italia?
articles.summary: La risposta non è univoca, a causa di diversi fattori, ed è stata strumentalizzata da gruppi ultraconservatori per alimentare la propria propaganda
articles.preview: Quanti sono i femminicidi in Italia? Da quando è stato introdotto il nuovo reato di femminicidio, nel dicembre 2025, la risposta è ancor meno univoca. Nei primi sei mesi del 2026, il ministero dell’Interno ha registrato 8 casi, mentre l’Osservatorio Non Una Di Meno (NUDM), movimento femminista e transfemminista italiano, ne ha conteggiati 39. Una discrepanza statistica che ha iniziato ben presto a girare sui social per negare o comunque minimizzare il fenomeno del femminicidio.
articles.body:
Quanti sono i femminicidi in Italia? Da quando è stato introdotto il nuovo reato di femminicidio, nel dicembre 2025, la risposta è ancor meno univoca. Nei primi sei mesi del 2026, il ministero dell’Interno ha registrato 8 casi, mentre l’Osservatorio Non Una Di Meno (NUDM), movimento femminista e transfemminista italiano, ne ha conteggiati 39. Una discrepanza statistica che ha iniziato ben presto a girare sui social per negare o comunque minimizzare il fenomeno del femminicidio. Secondo la tesi di pagine e profili dichiaratamente antifemministi o ultraconservatori, infatti, sarebbero i movimenti che si battono per i diritti delle donne a gonfiare i dati a fini propagandistici, inventandosi un’emergenza che in realtà non esiste.

Chi ha ragione? Per capirlo occorre analizzare entrambi i dati, chiedendosi prima di tutto come vengono raccolti e classificati.

Perché i dati sono differenti

Nei primi sei mesi del 2026, il report su omicidi volontari e femminicidi del ministero dell’Interno registra 146 vittime di omicidio (di cui 34 di sesso femminile). Tra queste, 46 persone (27 le donne) sono state uccise in ambito familiare o affettivo, di cui 22 da partner o ex partner. Tra le persone uccise da partner o ex, le donne sono 19 su 22, cioè più dell’86 per cento.

A fronte di questi dati, lo stesso report segnala 8 casi di femminicidio, tutti relativi a donne uccise da partner o ex. Gli altri 19 casi di omicidio in ambito familiare o affettivo con vittime di sesso femminile – e in particolare i restanti 11 casi di donne uccise da partner o ex – sono conteggiati invece come omicidi volontari.

Come spiega lo stesso report, il numero degli omicidi volontari e dei femminicidi registrato dal ministero dell’Interno corrisponde a quello dei procedimenti penali avviati in base ai rispettivi articoli del codice penale. Si tratta quindi di dati operativi, che fotografano la situazione giudiziaria del delitto nel periodo preso in considerazione e sono quindi soggetti a possibili variazioni in base agli sviluppi delle indagini. Col proseguimento del percorso investigativo, quindi, il giudice per le indagini preliminari può sia confermare il reato di omicidio volontario sia modificarlo in femminicidio, o viceversa.

Diversi sono i numeri registrati dall’Osservatorio Non Una Di Meno, perché diversi sono i criteri di raccolta e classificazione. Il movimento femminista e transfemminista non ha come punto di riferimento la formulazione giuridica del reato, bensì la sua definizione sociologica, maturata in decenni di ricerca sociale: il femminicidio è un delitto di potere, strumento estremo di controllo di una donna da parte di un uomo, molto spesso all’apice di un’escalation di violenza all’interno di una relazione fondata sulla discriminazione, sul possesso e sul sopruso.

L’Osservatorio – il cui nome completo è Osservatorio Nazionale Femminicidi Lesbicidi Transcidi – monitora quindi le cronache online e cartacee di media nazionali e locali per intercettare tutti quegli omicidi che rispecchiano tali caratteristiche. Per questo, come si legge nel suo comunicato di lancio nel novembre del 2021, prende in considerazione anche gli omicidi di persone trans per motivi riconducibili a relazioni di potere maschilista e violenza di genere, così come i suicidi e in generale le morti causate da violenze pregresse. La statistica include infine anche eventuali casi in corso di accertamento.

A partire da questi criteri, tra i 39 casi intercettati nei primi sei mesi del 2026, Non Una Di Meno individua 35 femminicidi, 1 transcidio e 3 episodi in corso di accertamento. Prendendo in considerazione unicamente i femminicidi, si tratta di un solo caso in più rispetto alla cifra dichiarata dal presidente della Repubblica Sergio Mattarella il 17 settembre 2026, nel corso della sua visita alla Stanza Rosa dell’Ospedale Misericordia di Grosseto, prima struttura sanitaria a sperimentare nel 2009 il Codice Rosa per tutte le vittime di violenza. I 34 casi nominati da Mattarella potrebbero semplicemente conteggiare come singolo episodio il duplice femminicidio che NUDM riporta invece due volte, trattandosi di due vittime.

Per ogni delitto conteggiato, l’Osservatorio raccoglie e rende pubbliche quasi una quarantina di informazioni dettagliate, relative sia alla vittima che al presunto colpevole, con l’obiettivo esplicito di fornire maggiori strumenti di comprensione e quindi di contrasto del fenomeno.

L’importanza di saper intercettare le dinamiche delle violenza di genere

A questo punto, per capire la disparità tra i dati del ministero dell’Interno e di Non Una Di Meno, occorre prendere in considerazione anche un altro aspetto: la mancata conoscenza e quindi intercettazione delle dinamiche della violenza di genere in ambito giudiziario. Una lacuna attestata da anni di studi, ricerche e report.

Il Rapporto sulla violenza di genere e domestica nella realtà giudiziaria, presentato nel 2022 dalla Commissione di inchiesta del Senato sul femminicidio e la violenza di genere, segnalava una sostanziale sottovalutazione del fenomeno causata anche da una carente formazione degli operatori coinvolti. Descrivendo un quadro complessivo di difficoltà e resistenze, pure di natura culturale, il report riconosce lo sforzo formativo e organizzativo compiuto da una parte minoritaria della magistratura ed evidenzia l’esistenza di esperienze virtuose all’interno di alcuni tribunali, ma sottolinea quanto questo non sia ancora sufficiente per intercettare e contrastare il fenomeno in modo capillare ed efficace.

Una maggiore formazione dei giudici sarebbe fondamentale anche per ridurre il rischio di condizionamenti dovuti a pregiudizi personali. Come spiega la sociologa Barbara Poggio dell’Università di Trento, spesso le sentenze contengono stereotipi di genere, per cui vengono poi ribaltate dalla Corte di Cassazione o diventano motivo di condanna dell’Italia da parte della Corte europea dei diritti dell’uomo.

Proprio uno studio su 370 sentenze di omicidi volontari di donne andati a giudizio tra il 2010 e il 2016, realizzato dalla sociologa Alessandra Dino dell’Università di Palermo, ha confermato che il riconoscimento del movente di genere non può essere dato per scontato, perché inquirenti e giudici sono necessariamente influenzati anche dal sentire comune.

La conseguenza – come rileva anche uno studio di Teresa Bene, docente di diritto processuale penale all’Università di Napoli – è che ancora oggi il sistema giudiziario tende a minimizzare la violenza, deresponsabilizzare gli autori e colpevolizzare le vittime, ostacolando così il pieno riconoscimento del fenomeno.

A prescindere dalla formazione e dai bias degli operatori coinvolti, comunque, rimane un fatto. Provare con certezza che una donna è stata uccisa come atto di odio, discriminazione, prevaricazione, controllo, possesso o dominio in quanto donna, o come limitazione delle sue libertà individuali oppure ancora in relazione al rifiuto di una relazione affettiva – come vuole il nuovo reato di femminicidio – non è così scontato. Anche perché una delle caratteristiche della violenza di genere, come confermano ad esempio varie ricerche sugli accessi al pronto soccorso, è proprio il suo essere sommersa. Talmente taciuta dalle vittime stesse, che spesso si trovano in una sorta di paralisi traumatica e cognitiva causata dalla violenza cronica, da non essere raccontata nemmeno ai familiari e agli amici più stretti.

La mancanza di una banca dati pubblica

Per portare davvero alla luce un fenomeno tanto complesso, la legge 53 del 2022, approvata all’unanimità in Parlamento, ha istituito una banca dati pubblica in cui dovrebbero confluire numerose e dettagliate informazioni provenienti dai ministeri dell’Interno, della Giustizia e della Salute, oltre che dai servizi sociali. Grazie a statistiche complete e integrate, si assicurerebbe così un adeguato monitoraggio del fenomeno, fondamentale per la progettazione di politiche di prevenzione e contrasto adeguate.

Ma dal 2022 è tutto fermo perché mancano i decreti attuativi, tuttora richiesti a gran voce da una petizione promossa da varie realtà tra cui la rete D.i.Re – Donne in rete contro la violenza, la più grande associazione nazionale italiana che riunisce i centri antiviolenza e le case rifugio gestiti da organizzazioni di donne.

Nel frattempo, le statistiche continueranno a restituire dati diversi. Una discrepanza che diventa pericolosa, se viene strumentalizzata per restituire solo un piccolo pezzo della realtà.

articles.title: Falsi giornali locali e slopaganda: cos’è successo nella campagna elettorale per le midterm
articles.summary: Sia democratici che repubblicani hanno finanziato siti “pink slime” e pubblicato video IA per attaccare gli avversari
articles.preview: Negli Stati Uniti, in vista delle elezioni di metà mandato (“midterm”) del 3 novembre 2026, vinte dai Democratici, vari gruppi con grandi risorse finanziarie hanno creato siti di finte testate giornalistiche locali indipendenti, con nomi credibili come “Ohio Pulse” o “Iowa Voice”, per pubblicare contenuti di parte e promuovere una narrazione favorevole al proprio partito e ai propri candidati.
articles.body:
Negli Stati Uniti, in vista delle elezioni di metà mandato (“midterm”) del 3 novembre 2026, vinte dai Democratici, vari gruppi con grandi risorse finanziarie hanno creato siti di finte testate giornalistiche locali indipendenti, con nomi credibili come “Ohio Pulse” o “Iowa Voice”, per pubblicare contenuti di parte e promuovere una narrazione favorevole al proprio partito e ai propri candidati.

Questi siti, chiamati in gergo “pink slime” (il nome deriva dalla poltiglia rosa di carne usata come additivo alimentare), si sono concentrati principalmente sugli Stati chiave, importanti per ottenere la maggioranza al Congresso.

Come rivelato da NewsGuard, progetto internazionale di monitoraggio dei media e della disinformazione, a investire in questa tecnica disinformativa sono stati sia democratici sia repubblicani che, oltre a creare questi siti web, hanno rilanciato e sponsorizzato gli articoli di storie false sui social media così da raggiungere un pubblico più ampio.

Ad esempio, quest’anno l’organizzazione senza scopo di lucro American Independent Media ha creato cinque nuovi siti, che si vanno ad aggiungere alla sua rete di 12 testate fittizie, per pubblicare e promuovere una prospettiva democratica, anche se non esplicitamente dichiarata. I nuovi siti di “finti giornali locali” producono articoli negativi sull’amministrazione Trump e le sue politiche e coprono ognuno uno Stato preciso: Florida, Carolina del Nord, Iowa, Alaska e Maine, tutti Stati cruciali per l’elezione del Congresso. Da gennaio, American Independent Media e un’altra organizzazione no-profit a cui è associata hanno speso circa 400mila dollari per promuovere gli articoli a favore del Partito Democratico su Facebook e Instagram, secondo i dati pubblicitari di Meta visionati da NewsGuard. Post che hanno totalizzato circa 40 milioni di visualizzazioni.

I siti “pink slime” sono arrivati anche su TIkTok. In particolare Courier Newsroom, una rete di 20 siti di informazione incentrati sulla politica locale e finanziato con milioni di dollari provenienti da gruppi liberali e vicini al Partito Democratico, ha creato 21 account TikTok riuscendo a raggiungere un’audience di oltre 4 milioni di follower e raccogliendo quasi 700 milioni di “mi piace”.

Anche One Nation, un’altra organizzazione no-profit affiliata al Senate Leadership Fund – un comitato di azione politica (PAC) che mira a eleggere senatori repubblicani – ha adottato la stessa tecnica manipolatoria e disinformativa. Nel 2026, come riporta la newsletter Popular Information, One Nation ha lanciato online sei siti conservatori che fingono di essere giornali locali indipendenti. Uno di questi è Alaska Navigator, i cui articoli mettono in luce solo ed esclusivamente il senatore repubblicano Dan Sullivan.

One Nation, si legge ancora nella newsletter, ha speso decine di migliaia di dollari in annunci di Meta per far sì che gli abitanti dello Stato dell’Alaska vedessero gli articoli di Alaska Navigator. Articoli e post social che, però, distorcono la realtà. Un articolo sulla lotta al fentanyl, un oppioide sintetico molto potente, è stato promosso con un annuncio che dichiarava l’esistenza di una «Nuova legge per contrastare il traffico di fentanyl, sostenuta da Dan Sullivan». In realtà, spiega l’autore Judd Legum di Popular Information, l’unica legge menzionata nell’articolo era l’HALT Fentanyl Act che, seppur sostenuta da Sullivan, è stata firmata ed è entrata in vigore nel luglio 2025.

Il grosso problema dei siti “pink slime” è che confondono spesso i lettori, ignari di leggere notizie di parte e spesso false, convinti di leggere, invece, contenuti giornalistici affidabili. NewsGuard riporta che un vero giornale dell’Alaska, Juneau Independent, è stato confuso con il falso “Alaska Independent”, tanto da dover spiegare apertamente ai propri lettori di non avere alcun legame con il sito “pink slime” finanziato da gruppi democratici per sostenere la campagna elettorale dell’ex deputata democratica Mary Peltola.

La tecnica di utilizzare siti fittizi di parte con tutte le caratteristiche per sembrare veri e propri giornali locali non è una novità delle midterm del 2026. Durante la campagna elettorale per le elezioni del 2024, ad esempio, NewsGuard aveva individuato circa mille siti “pink slime”, ma sono almeno venti anni che contenuti del genere circolano nel panorama informativo elettorale statunitense. La differenza in queste elezioni di metà mandato 2026 è che i siti “pink slime” sono ora citati dai chatbot di intelligenza artificiale come presunte fonti affidabili. Un’analisi di NewsGuard ha infatti individuato che i principali chatbot IA menzionano questi giornali fittizi di parte in quasi la metà delle risposte alle domande degli utenti sui temi e sui candidati delle midterm di cui si sono occupati i siti “pink slime”.

Nell’esperimento di NewsGuard basato su 7 chatbot, i chatbot IA hanno citato siti “pink slime” insieme ad altre fonti nel 48,2 per cento delle loro risposte, mentre sono stati l’unica fonte citata nel 7,7 per cento dei casi. Solo una risposta, su un totale di 168 domande, ha evidenziato la natura parziale della fonte. La strategia dei siti “pink slime” di presentare dei temi di parte come notizie neutrali e imparziali è riuscita ad amplificarsi grazie ai chatbot, sempre più utilizzati dagli utenti per informarsi su argomenti come le elezioni.

A ulteriore conferma del fatto che i siti “pink slime” si stanno insinuando nel dibattito politico e nell’ecosistema mediatico statunitense, i candidati e i comitati politici li hanno citati come fonti indipendenti nei propri spot di campagna elettorale, soprattutto in Iowa, Ohio e Alabama. Ad esempio, il comitato d’azione politica liberale Government that Works ha diffuso uno spot per screditare Ashley Hinson, candidata repubblicana alle elezioni per il Senato degli Stati Uniti in Iowa, collegandola a politiche che minacciano lo stile di vita rurale degli abitanti dell’Iowa, e promuovendo al contempo il suo avversario democratico Josh Turek (che si è aggiudicato il seggio). Nello spot appare una didascalia che riprende un articolo del sito “pink slime” Iowa Starting Line intitolato “Josh Turek lancia un piano per l’Iowa rurale”. Iowa Starting Line fa parte di Courier Newsroom, la già citata rete di 20 siti di informazione con legami finanziari a gruppi allineati con il Partito Democratico.

L’arrivo della slopaganda politica

A caratterizzare le campagne elettorali delle midterm del 2026, oltre ai falsi giornali di parte sponsorizzati sui social, c’è stato anche un aumento di spot politici e pubblicitari realizzati con i software di IA generativa per elogiare alcuni candidati e ridicolizzare gli avversari. Contenuti caricaturali e parodie iper-realistiche racchiudibili nel termine slopaganda, che unisce “AI slop”, ovvero la spazzatura da intelligenza artificiale, a “propaganda”. Una strategia comunicativa iniziata dal presidente USA Donald Trump, che da circa un anno ha fatto e sta ancora facendo un ampio uso di meme e immagini IA nei propri social personali e in quelli istituzionali.

Lo scorso aprile un comitato d’azione politica repubblicano ha diffuso uno spot creato con l’IA dell’avversario democratico Sherrod Brown (che ha vinto il seggio al Senato in Ohio) come ospite indesiderato alla fine di una festa di compleanno, intento a mangiare una torta mentre tutti gli invitati se ne sono andati. «Sherrod Brown è ancora in giro. L’abbiamo cacciato dopo 50 anni di carriera politica, ma lui proprio non se ne vuole andare», narra una voce fuori campo.

Un deepfake di James Talarico, candidato democratico al Senato in Texas e vincitore delle elezioni, compare in uno spot condiviso dal suo avversario nonché Procuratore generale del Texas Ken Paxton mentre scrive “La Bibbia del Re James Talarico” e fa affermazioni sul genere e sulla religione, come “Dio è non binario e non era cristiano”. Frasi che Talarico ha realmente dichiarato, ma che sono state decontestualizzate.

Sia Sherrod Brown che James Talarico sono stati tra l’altro vittima di un’operazione di interferenza russa che, tramite falsi servizi giornalistici televisivi manipolati con l’IA, ha cercato di minare la reputazione di vari candidati democratici. In questo caso Brown e Talarico erano stati falsamente accusati di violenza sessuale.

Un’altra vittima della slopaganda è stato Abdul El-Sayed, candidato al Senato del Michigan che ha battuto il repubblicano Mike Rogers. Uno spot da 30 secondi pubblicato da Rogers (poi cancellato) mostrava l’avversario El-Sayed insieme a Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez e Zohran Mamdani nascosto in un cavallo di Troia con addosso uno stendardo con scritto «certamente non comunismo» e che viene trascinato all’interno dello Stato del Michigan. El-Sayed, oltre a questo genere di contenuti è stato vittima anche di false notizie e insulti islamofobi, perpetrati ai massimi livelli del governo statunitense, compreso il presidente Donald Trump, che ha ripetutamente deriso il suo nome e lo ha definito un sostenitore degli jihadisti.

Il candidato repubblicano alla carica di Governatore di New York Bruce Blakeman ha pubblicato un video di un minuto contro l’avversaria democratica Kathy Hochul, che si è riconfermata Governatrice alle elezioni, in cui viene contestata dai cittadini per le tasse troppo alte; il video è ambientato in un mondo di personaggi Lego. In un altro video di campagna elettorale, pubblicato sempre da Blakeman, appaiono le caricature di Hochul e del sindaco di New York Zohran Mamdani mentre “distribuiscono nuove tasse” ai cittadini.

Blakeman ha difeso i suoi spot affermando che erano chiaramente etichettati come generati con l’intelligenza artificiale (un disclaimer che compare a inizio video, ndr) e che si inseriscono in una lunga tradizione di satira e parodia nella politica americana.

Ma per Scott Babwah Brennen, direttore del Center on Technology Policy dell’Università di New York, la “slopaganda” viene utilizzata per «comunicare verità più profonde piuttosto che verità fattuali», il che significa che potrebbe plasmare la percezione dell’ideologia di un candidato e potrebbe «influenzare la fiducia degli elettori».

Stando al Wesleyan Media Project, che monitora la pubblicità politica, durante la campagna elettorale per le midterm sono stati creati, al 29 ottobre, quasi 300 annunci pubblicitari generati o co-creati con l’intelligenza artificiale, per cui sono stati spesi oltre 187 milioni di dollari. Un dato che probabilmente è sottostimato poiché non tiene conto degli annunci politici generati con l’IA sui social media e perché l’IA può essere difficile da individuare e non sempre viene dichiarata, ha commentato a USA Today Michael Franz, docente di scienze politiche al Bowdoin College e condirettore dell’istituto di ricerca della Wesleyan University. Di questi quasi 300 spot creati con l’IA, solo il 27 per cento contiene un’informativa sulla sua natura artificiale.

A livello federale non esiste una legge univoca che disciplini i deepfake, ma negli anni gli Stati hanno adottato diverse risoluzioni e leggi a riguardo. Alcuni hanno vietato la pubblicazione di deepfake nei giorni precedenti alle votazioni, mentre altri la consentono purché sia presente un disclaimer.

Come hanno scritto i ricercatori del Center on Technology Policy nel report Political Slopaganda, alle midterm 2026 «piuttosto che contenuti generati dall’IA creati per sembrare autentici e destinati a ingannare gli elettori, stiamo assistendo a un’esplosione di contenuti generati dall’IA che non sembrano nascondere la propria origine artificiale». E, sebbene possano ingannare alcuni elettori in determinati casi, «questi contenuti sembrano progettati per raggiungere altri fini: piuttosto che ingannevole, la slopaganda politica sembra mirare maggiormente a essere umoristica, satirica o ad attirare l’attenzione».

Un esempio citato dal rapporto è lo spot di un comitato di azione politica repubblicano pensato per attaccare il sostegno del democratico James Talarico alle persone giovani transgender. Nel video IA, Talarico balla in abito da donna cantando una versione parodistica di “My Favorite Things” rielaborata per parlare di somministrare ormoni alle ragazze «fino a fargli crescere i baffi». «L’obiettivo non è probabilmente quello di far credere alla gente che Talarico abbia cantato la canzone», scrivono i ricercatori, «piuttosto quello di suscitare negli spettatori una certa reazione riguardo alle priorità dei Democratici e al modo in cui questi ultimi definiscono la mascolinità».

La slopaganda politica però, per gli esperti, «è probabilmente più efficace nel mobilitare gli elettori o nel raccogliere fondi che nell’influenzare la selezione dei candidati». Per i ricercatori, la slopaganda ha comunque un impatto importante, perché può minare ulteriormente la fiducia nelle istituzioni e può esacerbare la polarizzazione tra i partiti politici.

articles.title: US offers $20m reward for information about Iran's nuclear programme
articles.summary: Donald Trump has repeatedly raised the prospecting of renewing strikes against Iran's nuclear facilities.
articles.preview: The US has announced a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear programme. The State Department's Rewards for Justice is also offering to potentially relocate the person who provides such details. President Donald Trump claimed last year that Iran's nuclear facilities had been "completely and totally obliterated" following a bombing campaign by the US and Israel. Iran insists its nuclear programme is peaceful and that it has no intention of developing a nuclear weapon.
articles.body:
The US has announced a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear programme.

The State Department's Rewards for Justice is also offering to potentially relocate the person who provides such details.

President Donald Trump claimed last year that Iran's nuclear facilities had been "completely and totally obliterated" following a bombing campaign by the US and Israel.

Iran insists its nuclear programme is peaceful and that it has no intention of developing a nuclear weapon.

Meanwhile, the US military says it is setting up a task force to enhance Washington's efforts to restrict Iran's movement of weapons and sanctioned material across its borders.

The US military's Central Command (Centcom) said Task Force Iron Gate would operate from Tampa, Florida, and would work with other US government agencies.

As well as the movement of weapons, it will also focus on dual-use and illegal revenue streams.

Centcom estimates that its naval blockade of Iran's ports has prevented the country from exporting more than $25bn in crude oil.

A US State Department statement about its multi-million dollar reward said it was offering the money for information about the Iranian programme, including "facilities, equipment and associated personnel".

It said Iran's "lack of compliance with the IAEA [the International Atomic Energy Agency] on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like [nuclear] centrifuges".

Centrifuges are needed to produce enriched uranium, which can be used to make reactor fuel for civilian use but also for nuclear weapons if enriched to around 90% purity or higher.

There had been mounting speculation that the US might resume significant strikes in Iran after the midterm elections, though Trump told reporters, prior to the polls, that he was in "no rush" to do so.

In an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms, the president also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme.

This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump said.

The president has repeatedly threatened to bomb the suspected underground site on previous occasions.

However, both Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have said public opposition to the war on Iran fuelled heavy losses for their Republican Party in this week's midterm elections, which has led to speculation the White House may no longer seek an escalation in the conflict.

On Friday, Trump insisted that Iran was keen to end the eight-month conflict with the US, stressing the damage to Tehran's economy and military.

"We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said.

Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.

Iranian negotiators had discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

articles.title: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.summary: Weeks of coalition talks could follow after preliminary results pointed to a highly divided national parliament.
articles.preview: There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show. Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
articles.body:
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.

Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.

But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".

The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.

Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests, on 5.

The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.

Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".

He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."

Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."

Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".

More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.

But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.

They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests.

- New Zealand election 2026: What you need to know

- Published27 October

The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.

It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.

Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."

Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".

"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.

Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.

The Greens â who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops â saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.

Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders

"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.

More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.

New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.

Each voter makes two choices â for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

articles.summary: IRGC spokesman announces lifting of restrictions on Iranian missiles Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards has said that it has lifted restrictions on the range of Iran's missiles. IRGC spokesman, Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi reportedly made the comments at a press conference on Saturday, in response to question regarding the country's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei's warning to the US against further attacks on the country. Khamenei had previously said during a meeting with senior military commanders, that any renewed US or Israeli attck would be met with "with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response". The leader also reportedly ordered an update of Iran's military target database. According to Tasnim news agency, Mohebbi was asked on Saturday whether Khamenei's comments meant that limits on the range of Iranian missiles had been removed. He responded : "This restriction has been lifted for us". “Our duty is to show our capabilities on the battlefield,” he added.

articles.body:
November 7, 2026

18,000 people gathered in Frankfurt to show support for Reza Pahlavi, the son of the Iranian monarch ousted in 1979. Factions in the opposition have accused him of not distancing himself from his father's rule.

Iranian opposition leader Reza Pahlavi on Saturday received a "Freedom Prize" in Frankfurt in the central German state of Hesse.

Some 18,000 people rallied to show support for Reza Pahlavi, according to a police statement.

The event was held at St Paul's Church. The building hosted the Germany's first-ever elected parliament in 1848-1849, known as the Frankfurt Assembly.

Pahlavi is the son of the last shah of Iran, Mohammed Reza Pahlavi, an autocrat who fled into exile after being deposed in a 1979 revolution.

The 1979 revolution was followed by the transformation of Iran into an Islamic republic and the consolidation of power around the Shiite Muslim clergy.

Pahlavi was handed the prize by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which is tied to the pro-business Free Democratic Party (FDP).

What did Reza Pahlavi say about the prize?

Pahlavi said that Iran "is a country not waiting to be taught democracy, this is a country being prevented from practicing it."

"A people ready to die for the right to vote is willing to exercise the right to vote," he said.

Rights groups say thousands were killed in a government crackdown on protests in January.

"You could not have chosen a people who better understand the meaning of the word 'freedom,'" he said.

He also stressed that he was receiving the prize only as a "trustee" until a democratically-elected government comes to power in Iran.

"I hold it only temporarily," he said. "One day I will place it in the hands of its rightful owners, not on foreign soil but in the capital, Tehran."

The speech was accompanied by chants of "Long live the shah, long live Iran!" from the crowd.

Pahlavi has in the past offered to lead a transitional government in the event of a democratic transition in the West Asian country and has said he does not aim to use this proposed position to reinstate the Iranian monarchy under his father's dynasty, instead planning to leave the decision to a later referendum.

Iranians criticize Freedom Prize for Pahlavi prince

While Pahlavi has emerged as a figurehead for factions within the anti-government protest movement, others have criticized him for his vocal support for Israel and have accused him of failing to distance himself from his father's autocratic rule.

Around 200 prisoners held in Iran signed a letter protesting Pahlavi's receipt of the prize, Sahar Sanaie, spokeswoman for the Society for German-Iranians in Hesse, was cited by the AFP news agency as saying.

The letter described him as the symbol of a "bygone dictatorship."

The Frankfurt branches of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the environmentalist Greens boycotted the event and said he could not be considered a legitimate representative of the Iranian people.

Meanwhile, the socialist Left Party argued that the church could not by used as a venue for the event due to Frankfurt city statutes that prevent the use of places of worship for political gatherings.

articles.title: After victory in the midterms, what next for US Democrats?
articles.summary: Donald Trump's Republican party has lost its majority in both chambers of the US Congress. But the president still has a lot of power — and the Democrats have yet to agree on how best to use theirs.
articles.preview: November 7, 2026 Donald Trump's Republican party has lost its majority in both chambers of the US Congress. But the president still has a lot of power — and the Democrats have yet to agree on how best to use theirs. A "blue wave" has rolled across the United States. The Democrats scored a decisive victory in the midterm elections on November 3, wresting the majority from President Donald Trump's Republicans in both the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
articles.body:
November 7, 2026

Donald Trump's Republican party has lost its majority in both chambers of the US Congress. But the president still has a lot of power — and the Democrats have yet to agree on how best to use theirs.

A "blue wave" has rolled across the United States. Some are even calling it a "blue tsunami." The Democrats scored a decisive victory in the midterm elections on November 3, wresting the majority from President Donald Trump's Republicans in both the US House of Representatives and the Senate. They also won gubernatorial elections in former Republican strongholds such as Texas.

Pictures from Tuesday evening show Democrat politicians and supporters across the country celebrating, hugging, even weeping with joy. However, as the White House reminded Americans in a post on X the day after the elections: "Trump is still your president."

Trump has the power to veto any proposed legislation Congress puts before him, and his veto can only be overruled by a two-thirds majority. Also, in the past he has, on occasion, simply ignored the Congress's decision.

How much power do the Democrats have?

Patrick Malone, professor at the public administration and policy department at American University in Washington DC, told DW that a presidential veto is not necessarily the end of the matter — even though the Democrats don't have a two-thirds majority in either Congressional chamber.

"There are Republicans, especially on the House side, who are not going to want to tie themselves that closely to Trump anymore," says Malone. "The Republicans that survived had a very strong message sent to them. It would be illogical and foolish for them to point to a neighboring district [that turned blue] and say, 'Well, that can't happen here.'"

For that reason, Malone predicts that Republicans and Democrats may come together to overrule a Trump veto. "It could happen very easily."

Will Trump be impeached again?

A question at the front of many people's minds is: Might the Democrats make another attempt at impeachment? One possible basis for this would be that Trump started the war with Iran without congressional approval. The US Constitution says only Congress has the power to declare war. But as commander-in-chief, the president also has a degree of military authority. How far this extends without Congressional approval is legally disputed.

From January 2027, Democrats will have the simple majority required to bring charges against him in the House of Representatives. They will not, however, be able to muster the two-thirds majority in the Senate that would be needed for a conviction and Trump's removal from office. Some Democrats say it is nonetheless imperative that the impeachment process be initiated, as a way of keeping the president in check.

Others remain skeptical. "If we make Donald Trump the center of our focus, we will lose this moment in history," the Democratic senator Cory Booker said. "We need to deal with the American people's problems."

This does not mean that Democrats won't try to launch investigations into Trump, or into members of his family or government. Quite the reverse. Malone believes the Democrats in Congress take their control function very seriously and will definitely initiate investigations. These, he says, serve a purpose beyond the documented outcome: "Another thing about Congressional investigations: They have a much stronger impact on public opinion than on legislation. They catch people's attention."

Will Hegseth be sacked as secretary of defense?

While Trump will most likely get to keep his job, Pete Hegseth might be about to lose his. Observers assume the Democrats will demand a different secretary of defense. "There's a lot of speculation about what's going to happen to Pete Hegseth," says Brandon Conradis, a former DW journalist who is now an editor at Bloomberg Government in Washington DC. Whether Trump will actually fire Hegseth is a decision for the president. All the Democrats can do is exert political pressure.

From January onward, the Democrats will have a majority in Congress, which is where decisions are made on how government funds are spent. Conradis says one possibility for the Democrats to get their way would be to link the financing of Trump's pet projects to specific conditions. "One thing Democrats might do is say, 'Look, if you want more funding for these conflicts, Pete Hegseth needs to go.'"

As secretary of defense, Hegseth is being held at least partially responsible for the US's relative lack of success in the war with Iran. This could also be a reason for Trump to fire him.

Democrats not a unified bloc

After their success in the midterms, the Democrats have been enjoying a brief moment of unity. But Malone says it won't last. "The Democratic Party was unified for maybe 24, 36 hours. Now they're not really going to unify for a bit."

Unlike Germany, the US does not have governing coalitions at the federal level. There are, however, various political groupings within the Democratic Party itself. On the left wing of the political spectrum there are the progressive Democrats, including, among others, the prominent young representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. "[Progressives] have very aggressive policy ideas, whether it be environment or social programs," comments Malone.

In the middle are the mainstream liberal Democrats, who see themselves as politically pragmatic and good at compromising. But there are also moderates. "This is an important group on the Democratic side," Malone says. "There were a lot of Democrats [in the midterms] who won elections in former red districts or really, really conservative blue districts. They won't be able to go back to their districts and say, 'Look, AOC wants this.'"

It will be no easy task for Democrats in Congress to agree on one clear direction. But many believe that it's vital that they do. "They're going to have to figure out a positive governing agenda that they can all agree on," says Malone. Just opposing Trump won't be enough for the Democrats to sustain their current success, the pundit argues.

articles.title: Who is Hakeem Jeffries, the Democrat poised to become House speaker?
articles.summary: Likely to become the first Black House speaker, Jeffries faces pressure from progressives over Trump and Israel.
articles.preview: Likely to become the first Black House Speaker, Jeffries faces pressure from progressives over Trump and Israel. With Democrats’ decisive victory in the United States’ midterm elections on Tuesday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York is on the verge of making history as the first Black speaker of the US House of Representatives.
articles.body:
Likely to become the first Black House Speaker, Jeffries faces pressure from progressives over Trump and Israel.

With Democrats’ decisive victory in the United States’ midterm elections on Tuesday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York is on the verge of making history as the first Black speaker of the US House of Representatives.

For the 56-year-old congressman, it would be the culmination of almost two decades in office, giving him a central role in Democrats’ efforts to rein in Republican US President Donald Trump in the final two years of his presidency.

Public pressure builds around Jeffries’ stance on Trump and Israel

But as Jeffries celebrated the “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats back into power the day after the election, some voters and those within the party were not convinced that the congressman, known for his cautious approach to politics and longstanding support for Israel, was the right man for the moment.

An online petition on Change.org calling on lawmakers to choose another speaker had collected more than 1 million signatures by Saturday afternoon, while several newly elected progressive lawmakers have not said whether they will support him.

“We believe the Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment,” the petition reads.

“This is not a foregone conclusion,” it continues, urging others to run for the job.

Jeffries, who has spent years cultivating relationships within the Democratic caucus, now finds himself at the centre of a bigger fight within the party, as its growing progressive wing pushes for a more confrontational approach to Trump and a break with some of the ideas that have defined the Democrats for decades as well as US support for Israel.

Jeffries’s Israel stance divides Democrats

Of all the sources of tension between Jeffries and his party’s progressive wing, the hardest divide to bridge may be over his longstanding support for Israel and ties to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).

At a conference hosted by the group in 2020, Jeffries opposed putting conditions on US aid to Israel and described Jerusalem as New York City’s “sixth borough”.

He has also been one of the top recipients of financial support from AIPAC and its network of donors, earning the nickname “AIPAC Shakur” from New York radio host Charlamagne tha God.

In a celebratory post after the elections congratulating the candidates it had supported, AIPAC singled out Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer by name.

But Jeffries’s steadfast support for Israel throughout its genocidal war on Gaza has put him increasingly at odds with his own party, and he recently signalled that his position may be changing.

In July, even as he voted against an amendment that would have cut $3.3bn in annual military aid to Israel, he acknowledged the need for a reset in US-Israel relations.

“A meaningful change in direction is needed,” he wrote in a letter to colleagues.

Jeffries appears to have the speakership all but secured, with no serious challenger emerging so far.

However, with Trump still in the White House, a party grappling with its own divisions, and voters expecting change on everything from the cost of living to the war on Iran, the bigger test for Jeffries will come once he is on the job.

From Brooklyn to Democratic leader

Jeffries grew up in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, in the 1970s and 1980s, as the neighbourhood was grappling with the crack cocaine epidemic.

“There was a lot of dysfunction and pain that surrounded the communities that I was raised in, but also a lot of love and compassion from family and friends, and community folks,” he told NYU Law in 2019.

The son of two social workers, Jeffries eventually became a lawyer, tracing his decision to pursue a career in law back to the 1992 riots that erupted in Los Angeles after four white police officers were acquitted in the beating of Rodney King, a Black man.

“It crystallized the fact that we still had a long way to go to eradicate social and racial injustice,” he said.

Jeffries went on to work as a corporate lawyer before entering politics, losing two runs for the New York State Assembly before winning a seat in 2006 and eventually being elected to Congress six years later.

In Washington, he helped broker a bipartisan criminal justice reform law signed by Trump in 2018. Two years later, during Trump’s first impeachment trial, he argued that Trump should be removed from office as one of seven House impeachment managers who presented the case to the US Senate.

Rising quickly through the Democratic ranks, Jeffries became caucus chair in 2019 before making history three years later, when he was unanimously chosen to succeed former Speaker Nancy Pelosi as the party’s House leader, becoming the first Black politician to lead a party in either chamber of Congress.

Can Jeffries unite his party?

Jeffries and Pelosi have been compared for their distinct leadership styles. While Pelosi was known for her commanding, top-down approach, Jeffries has built a reputation for quietly and deliberately building consensus among his colleagues.

That approach has frustrated some Democrats, who say Jeffries has been too reluctant to take firm positions and who question whether he is prepared to confront Trump and Republicans in Congress aggressively enough.

Those concerns were on display after Jeffries declared after the election that “the American people don’t want us to get even; they want us to get things done on their behalf.”

Among those who pushed back was left-wing political commentator Hasan Piker, who reposted a video of Jeffries’s comments, saying: “No, we definitely ARE looking for justice and accountability.”

Jeffries also faced criticism after reports emerged in August that he had privately met Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, who does not have a formal role in the administration but has been involved in diplomatic efforts in the Middle East and in Russia.

Jeffries defended the meeting, saying Kushner had requested it and that he had used it to discuss the affordability crisis. But critics argued that rather than meeting privately with Kushner, Jeffries should have been preparing to investigate his business dealings.

Ahead of the election, Axios reported on a plan by some incoming progressive lawmakers – informally known as “The Bloc” and including Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Melat Kiros of Colorado – to use the upcoming speaker vote to win concessions from Jeffries on issues such as Medicare for All, cutting funding for ICE, and weapons shipments to Israel.

That may be harder now that the Democrats have a comfortable majority, with Jeffries less dependent on progressive newcomers to secure the speakership. But the result also makes it harder for Jeffries to argue, as he has in the past, that Republican control of Congress is hindering the Democrats’ ability to advance their agenda and hold Trump accountable.

articles.body:
New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next government, after its nail-biting election failed to hand a decisive victory to either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc.

On preliminary results, the centre-right National party, led by the prime minister, Christopher Luxon, managed to secure enough seats to govern alongside its traditional coalition partners, the libertarian Act and populist New Zealand First parties.

But with some seats won by very slim margins, and special votes yet to be counted, that success is precarious, resulting in an election too close to call until official results are released on 27 November.

Special votes include overseas votes and ballots cast outside a voter’s electorate. In 2023, 600,000 such votes were made, 21% of the total. These votes tend to favour the left – in 2023, special votes resulted in Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) and the Greens gaining three seats between them.

With nearly 100% of the regular votes counted on Saturday night, National secured 42 seats, Act 13 and New Zealand First 12. The combined 67-seat majority is wafer thin, with the left bloc just three seats behind.

Speaking to a room full of the party faithful at Auckland’s Viaduct events centre just before midnight, Luxon said the results were “too close to call” and the special votes would need to be counted before negotiations could begin.

National was still the largest party in parliament, he said, and had “a pathway to forming the next government”. National pipped Labour by 0.02% in the party vote.

Labour, led by Chris Hipkins, secured 35 seats, while its traditional coalition partners the Greens won 16 and Te Pāti Māori five. Even with the seven seats from the centrist newcomer party, Opportunity, the left bloc is three seats short of forming a government.

Before a rowdy crowd of supporters at the Cosmopolitan Club in Upper Hutt, north of Wellington, Hipkins joked that New Zealand had spoken but “it may take a bit longer to work out what they’ve said”.

“As things stand tonight, it is clear that we are not going to know the shape of our next government for a little while longer yet,” Hipkins said, promising that Labour would get “straight to work” should the final count land in its favour.

The collapse of the two major parties, amid a sluggish economy and stubbornly high inflation, is feeding record support for the smaller parties, including Act, New Zealand First and the Greens. It is also helped propel Opportunity into parliament for the first time.

Opinion polls in the lead-up to the election had Opportunity placed to become the kingmaker. At this stage, the right bloc does not need the party to govern, but if special votes change the landscape, its predicted role could come to fruition.

Currently at 5.9%, the centrist party has met the threshold needed to enter parliament, a historic first. Since New Zealand adopted the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system in 1996, no new party has been able to meet that threshold – all the other minor parties have been born from MPs or groups splintering from larger parties.

The party’s leader, Qiulae Wong, told her supporters in Auckland she was “stoked”.

“It’s looking very promising for us,” she said. “Let’s just see how the rest of the votes fall.”

In New Zealand, voters cast two votes: one for an electorate MP and one for a party. The system is meant to produce a parliament that reflects each party’s share of the nationwide vote.

However, if New Zealanders vote for more electorate MPs from a particular party than their party vote would entitle them to, they get to keep the extra MPs in what is called an overhang.

National won more seats that its party support allows for, meaning it could gain an extra five seats to make up the balance.

That will be good news for its path to power, but comes with some significant trade-offs for the party. Four of its most senior ministers, including Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith, Chris Bishop and Gerry Brownlee, will not return to parliament because they did not win a seat, or the party didn’t win enough votes to bring in list-only MPs.

On the other side of the house, Te Pāti Māori picked up five overhang seats.

With all the extra seats, there could be 130 in the next parliament – a record under MMP – which means 65 seats are needed to form a coalition.

The country faces a two-week wait until special votes are announced, followed by the possibility of weeks of negotiations. Luxon said caretaker government conventions would apply in the meantime.

“For now, I want to tell New Zealanders that well-established caretaker conventions apply … The daily business of government will continue.”

articles.body:
Thanks for following the blog tonight. The election has ended without a clear winner. Here are the top news lines from what will go down as one of New Zealand’s closest elections in many decades.

Christopher Luxon’s National party and its right-leaning coalition partners are on the brink of a wafer-thin majority that could allow it to eke out a return to power.

The left-wing bloc, led by Labour’s Chris Hipkins, fell short of a majority.

Neither Luxon or Hipkins claimed victory or conceded defeat. Both acknowledged an expected wait before a governing coalition is negotiated.

A centrist newcomer, the Opportunity party, have entered parliament, polling above the 5% threshold. They could potentially be a kingmaker in a coalition.

Final results are expected on 27 November. Coalition talks will likely take weeks.

Hundreds of thousands of special votes are yet to be counted and could change the shape of parliament.

Saturday figures showed there could be a 130-seat parliament, with 66 seats needed for a majority.

Results suggested a coalition of National, Act and NZ First would hold 67 seats.

The 67 included 42 for National, 13 for Act and 12 for NZ First.

The left-bloc totalled 56 seats: Labour 35, Greens 16 and 5 for Te Pāti Māori.

Over the coming days and weeks we will get a sense of the magnitude of Qiulae Wong and the Opportunity party’s success tonight. Opportunity are currently projected to claim seven seats in parliament.

Wong has said that if she held the tiebreaker power, she was open to negotiating with either a conservative or a left-wing government and would deal first with whichever major party won the most votes.

The right-wing bloc might not need her, and Luxon has ruled out governing with Opportunity. Analysts say, however, that both major party leaders would likely answer the phone if Wong held the only path to power.

You can elle Duff.

With 0.56% support, Te Pāti Māori will be stoked with its result tonight, writes Jamie Tahana.

It seems odd, but the Māori party has spent the election deliberately asking people not to give them their party vote. Instead, they asked for electorate votes only.

Just a reminder, seven of the seats in New Zealand’s parliament are reserved for representatives of Māori voters – you can

The party’s co-leaders, Rawiri Waititi and Debbie Ngarewa-Packer, have comfortably won their respective seats of Waiariki and Te Tai Hauauru; Oriini Kaipara swept the Auckland seat of Tamaki Makaurau; Hana Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke, who hit international stardom for her haka in parliament, has cruised across the line in Hauraki-Waikato; while Aperahama Edwards holds a narrow lead over the Greens’ Hūhana Lydon in the far North seat of Te Tai Tokerau.

That’s five seats. But with a party vote so low, they will be five overhang seats.

Still, after a term that has seen plenty of in-fighting in Te Pāti Māori, there are signs of frustration in the Māori electorate, with Waititi and Ngarewa-Packer seeing significantly reduced majorities.

The Greens have fallen short of gaining their first ever Māori electorate, but across the seats party vote has risen to about 40%, making the party a significant force in Māori politics.

Labour, having been punished by the Māori electorate in 2023, has improved, particularly in terms of party vote, and has claimed a new MP in Mananui Ramsden, who won the country’s largest electorate, Te Tai Tonga.

So, hundreds of thousands of special votes are going to potentially change where things stand right now.

In his speech tonight, Luxon said 300,000 special votes were yet to be counted. Those votes, which will be counted and known by 27 November, typically sway left.

In the 2023 election there 600,000 special votes, and National dropped from 50 seats in the preliminary count to 48 seats.

In a 130-seat parliament, in which 66 seats are needed to govern, this is where things stand with 97% of the vote counted. However, special votes are still to be counted and the lay of the land will not be clear until 27 November.

Jamie Tahana has this hot-take on the Luxon speech:

It was a tough line to tread for a speech: National is the biggest party on current results – 29.30% – but Luxon has also led the party to one of its most unpopular points, only 0.1% ahead of Labour. Luxon has also lost some of his most senior and experienced MPs, which he conceded required “some tough phone calls”.

Luxon said, that because of the closeness of the result, and with special votes still to be counted, caretaker conventions will apply.

“For now, I want to tell New Zealanders that well established caretaker conventions apply … The daily business of government will continue.”

Caretaker convention basically means that while a new government is being formed, the incumbent government is in “caretaker” mode, which means it will carry on the normal business of governing.

Jamie Tahana notes that for Luxon to continue as prime minister, he will have to cobble together a three- or four-party coalition, from a weakened position compared to 2023.

In his speech, Luxon said: “Negotiations and compromises are going to be required … A number of races are still too close to call.”

Luxon called the election “too close to call”, and said “meaningful negotiations” for a new coalition government will start after the final results are known on 27 November.

“It looks like an MMP special,” he said. “It’s heartening to see that so far National is once again the largest party in parliament and we have a path to forming the next government.”

Luxon arrived to a crowd of about 700 raucous supporters chanting “three more years”. He was flanked by his wife Amanda and two children, waved and grinned as he descended a stairwell flanked in blue light.

A heavy music track - which could not be immediately identified through Shazam - thrummed as he walked down a long aisle, hugging supporters.

When he took the podium, Luxon conceded the election was “too close to call” but the crowd cheered as he announced National had secured the highest party count.

He went on to acknowledge Labour leader Chris Hipkins, and admonished supporters who booed Quilae Wong and Opportunity, saying it was “not the kiwi way”.

Luxon is also paying tribute to those high-ranking National MPs who find themselves out of a job tonight: Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith and Gerry Brownlee. “I want to thank you … for your years of service to our party”.

articles.title: Four things we learned this week about 2028 White House race
articles.summary: The seismic Democratic gains in Congress could shape the presidential election, so who had a good night and who's making moves?
articles.preview: Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race. Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump. But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010. No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.
articles.body:
Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.

Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.

But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.

No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.

Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.

The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways. Here are four takeaways.

1. Big winners in the midterms now have momentum

Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.

Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.

While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.

Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, swept aside his Republican challenger.

Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.

Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.

California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.

On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.

Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.

- Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff

- Published22 hours ago

- What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress

- Published3 days ago

2. JD Vance and Trump's allies under pressure

Exit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.

That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.

Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party.

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.

Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.

Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.

In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz, who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters.

"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.

Former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie was blunt in his assessment: "The Trump era is over."

3. Left and centre Democrats in fight for future

Both the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.

Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.

El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.

His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election.

"The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.

Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."

Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.

This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.

Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.

Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.

- Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide

- Published1 day ago

4. Support of Hispanic voters must be earned

Both parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.

Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds.

Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.

Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".

That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Global, a global communications and advisory firm.

"Neither party owns these voters," she said.

The Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.

Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend.

"Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said.

"After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

articles.title: Paraguay VP Alliana sworn is as president after predecessor impeached
articles.summary: Former Paraguayan Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president Friday to serve out the term of his predecessor, Santiago Peña, who was impeached earlier the same day for misconduct in office.
articles.preview: Paraguay Former Paraguayan Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president Friday to serve out the term of his predecessor, Santiago Peña, who was impeached earlier the same day for misconduct in office. Alliana was elected vice president of Paraguay as Peña's running mate in 2023. He should now serve out Peña's term, which runs until August 2028. In a unanimous vote, the 44 senators present voted to remove Peña for misconduct in office, bringing a dramatic end to one of South America's most stable presidencies.
articles.body:
Paraguay

Former Paraguayan Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as president Friday to serve out the term of his predecessor, Santiago Peña, who was impeached earlier the same day for misconduct in office.

Alliana was elected vice president of Paraguay as Peña's running mate in 2023. He should now serve out Peña's term, which runs until August 2028.

In a unanimous vote, the 44 senators present voted to remove Peña for misconduct in office, bringing a dramatic end to one of South America's most stable presidencies.

The verdict came just three days after regulators seized Ueno Bank, cutting nearly 3 million customers off from their savings and bank cards and setting off a political crisis.

Ousted Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was placed under house arrest Friday on suspicion of breach of trust, shortly after the Senate removed him from office over the collapse of a major bank tied to his government.

Prosecutors ordered that Peña be held at his home until he can be brought before their economic crimes and anti-corruption unit, according to a letter to the national police commander.

The attorney general's office confirmed to The Associated Press that he had been detained there.

The order also called for the arrest of Carlos Carvallo, the former central bank chief Peña appointed. It was not immediately clear whether Carvallo was in custody.

Lawmakers accused Peña of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending.

Peña has denied wrongdoing.

A veteran of the long-ruling conservative Colorado party, Alliana, 52, is a former governor of the southern province of Ñeembucú and a former speaker of the lower house.

He has not escaped the scandal entirely: Prosecutors are also investigating him, and on Thursday lawmakers shelved an opposition bid to impeach him.

Peña had submitted his resignation Thursday, but Congress did not accept it. His lawyers, Ricardo Preda and Adolfo Ferreiro, argued that lawmakers should have approved his departure instead of pressing ahead with the impeachment trial.

Public outrage has become more thunderous by the day.

As senators deliberated Friday, crowds of protesters demanding their frozen savings back and accountability for Ueno's failure marched through downtown Asunción.

articles.title: Ukraine: Russia hits Kyiv with airstrikes ahead of trilateral talks
articles.summary: The strikes hit a major bridge and energy facilities in the Kyiv region. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of trying to "push" Ukraine "into a blackout" ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi.
articles.preview: November 7, 2026 The strikes hit a major bridge and energy facilities in the Kyiv region. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of trying to "push" Ukraine "into a blackout" ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi. Russia launched strikes on Kyiv and surrounding areas overnight, Russian and Ukrainian authorities said on Saturday. Russia's Defense Ministry said the strikes hit the Northern Bridge and the Meridian Plant.
articles.body:
November 7, 2026

The strikes hit a major bridge and energy facilities in the Kyiv region. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of trying to "push" Ukraine "into a blackout" ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi.

Russia launched strikes on Kyiv and surrounding areas overnight, Russian and Ukrainian authorities said on Saturday.

Russia's Defense Ministry said the strikes hit the Northern Bridge and the Meridian Plant.

Moscow said that the bridge was being used by the Ukrainian military to transport weapons and military equipment, while the plant is used to produce Flamingo cruise missiles.

It said the strikes damaged several energy and industrial facilities in the Kyiv region, as well as an electricity substation in the neighboring Zhytomyr region and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.

What have Ukrainian authorities said about the attacks?

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed the strikes on the Northern Bridge, adding that the Ukrainian capital found itself in an "extremely difficult" situation regarding power, heating and water supplies. Overnight temperatures dropped to 0 degrees Celsius (32 degrees Fahrenheit) in the city.

The Kyiv region's governor, Tymur Tkachenko, said energy facilities in three of its districts had been hit.

Ukrainian authorities said that one person was killed and eight were wounded in the overnight attack.

In a statement on social media, president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles during the attack.

He said that Russia was trying to "push Kyiv … and the entire country into a blackout" and repeated his call for increased support from the United States.

Russia has stepped up airstrikes on Ukraine in recent months, targeting energy infrastructure and major cities, and more recently hitting bridges.

Strikes come ahead of Russia-Ukraine talks

The strikes come days before a fourth round of trilateral talks between Kyiv, Moscow and Washington in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates.

Previous rounds of US-brokered talks have failed to achieve any breakthroughs, with territorial and security questions remaining major points of contention.

On Friday, US President Donald Trump said the war could be close to being settled and that he envisioned a "big, beautiful agreement" with Moscow that involves "all of Europe."

Last Friday, a six-day local ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the southern Kherson region enabled the evacuation of some 800 residents.

The brief truce was brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.

articles.title: Political chaos in Somalia after court ruling against president's term extension
articles.summary: Somalia's political crisis is deepening, with the opposition accusing the president of sending troops to arrest the Supreme Court's chief justice after the tribunal declared an extension of his term "unlawful".
