articles.body:
Somalia

Mogadishu residents on Friday expressed mixed feelings after Somalia's Supreme Court ruled an extension of the president's term was "unlawful".

The country is mired in a deepening political crisis, with the opposition accusing President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud of sending troops to arrest the Supreme Court's chief justice.

"The Supreme Court is right and its decision is right. In the world, all people and governments abide by court decisions, and the rule of law must be respected," said Abdullahi Hassan Sheikh, a Mogadishu resident.

"I see the court decision as wrong because, when the new constitution was being approved, the court was operational," said Mohamed Farah Ahmed.

Somalia is dealing with multiple crises, with political rivalries that have descended into violent clashes, while the government loses international support for its fight against the powerful Islamist insurgent group, Al-Shabaab.

President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has tried to move Somalia towards fully democratic elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick their representatives.

But his opponents see the reforms as a power grab, especially after the president declared a "transition period" that gave him an extra year in office when his term ended in May.

Mohamud argues he was allowed to stay in office under constitutional amendments passed by parliament, to prepare for the first nationwide democratic elections in April and May 2027.

But the Supreme Court ruled on Thursday that they should never have applied to Mohamud's current term and he should have left office in May. It called for a new agreement between political parties within 30 days, and elections to be held within 90 days.

Before the ruling had even been published, the president's office announced on Facebook that he was dismissing the chief justice, Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, and appointing a replacement, because of "concerns... about the need for an efficient and fair judiciary".

The court responded that the president had no authority to fire the judge, accusing him of trying "to obstruct the administration of justice in the constitutional case filed before the Supreme Court".

A former prime minister, Hassan Ali Khaire, told reporters that the president had "launched an assault on the Supreme Court and deployed troops to its premises" on Thursday.

"The chief justice and lawyers are being pursued in their homes for arrest, have been subjected to torture, and the court's operations have been halted," he added.

His claims could not be verified by AFP, but images published by Somali media claimed to show military forces in the court's compound.

"Somalia stands at a dangerous juncture. The dismantling of our judiciary is a direct threat to the rule of law," said Ali Khaire. "I call on all sectors of Somali society to stand up now and defend Somalia's constitutionalism."

Security crisis

Most of the opposition and regional parties boycotted the vote on amending the constitution when it went to parliament in March, and some said they were barred from attending.

Violence broke out in the capital, Mogadishu, in June as political factions clashed over the issue.

The flare-up comes at a time when Somalia is also facing a security crisis related to the long-running insurgency by the Al-Qaeda-linked Al-Shabaab group that controls swathes of the country.

International donors, frustrated by the lack of progress against the militants and the endless political chaos, have been slashing funding for the international military mission that has been ongoing for almost 20 years.

Uganda, the biggest contributor to the African Union's force, announced this week that it was pulling out all troops by the end of 2027.

Washington has cut all donations to a critical United Nations logistics mission on which the military coalition relies.

articles.preview: Democrats’ sweep could urge Israel’s divided opposition to join forces and remove prime minister closely allied with Trump The Democrats’ sweep of Congress may make it easier for Israel’s splintered opposition to overcome deep internal divisions and form a coalition government, by increasing the urgency of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu, who has associated himself so closely with Donald Trump’s Republicans.
articles.body:
The Democrats’ sweep of Congress may make it easier for Israel’s splintered opposition to overcome deep internal divisions and form a coalition government, by increasing the urgency of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu, who has associated himself so closely with Donald Trump’s Republicans.

But as Israel took stock of the results, there was also a sense that the elections marked a longer-term shift in US politics that will make the job of any new Israeli leader far more difficult.

The United States provides Israel with critical military and diplomatic support, so nurturing bipartisan ties was the cornerstone of foreign policy for decades. Netanyahu ripped up that commitment to throw his lot in with the Republicans in general and Trump in particular.

The opposition had always attacked his decision as ill-judged. By the end of the week, they were warning that it was positively dangerous.

“These people aren’t against Israel,” prominent opposition politician Yair Lapid said of incoming Democratic lawmakers, urging his country to rebuild bridges. “They’re mainly against Netanyahu – for them, anything connected to him is toxic.”

“The easiest thing is to scream that ‘America is lost,’ because if it’s lost, you don’t have to work. That’s just not true. Not at all.”

Lapid laid out a plan to “rebuild trust” in the US, but it perhaps did more to demonstrate the scale of the problem than reassure Israelis.

His proposal of a transatlantic charm offensive by officials of a prospective new government drew a swift and sharp rebuke from the New York congressman-elect Brad Lander.

Lander, a Democrat who is Jewish and describes himself as a liberal Zionist, was detained in the occupied West Bank last month while joining Palestinians trying to harvest olives.

“Minister Lapid: As someone who won a seat in Congress last night, and who cares about Israel: you’re not listening to what American voters – Jewish and non-Jewish – are saying,” Lander wrote in a direct response.

“We aren’t starving for a barnstorming tour. We’re hungry to see respect for international law and human rights.”

In his exchange with Lapid, Lander also highlighted the arrest of journalist Abed Abu Shehada, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, as an example of how Israel violates international law. He drew a direct link with the ICE “regime of detention without charges, based on secret evidence, designed to intimidate and chill speech” that he said was rejected by US voters.

Abu Shehada was reportedly taken from his home by 15 masked security officials in a night-time raid, without an arrest warrant. Interrogators have only questioned him about a podcast interview with a public figure, lawyers acting for Abu Shehada said.

On Friday, Lander and two other incoming Jewish members of Congress, Daniel Bliss and Scott Wiener, wrote to Israel’s ambassador to the US calling for the immediate release of Abu Shehada.

“Detaining a reporter for conducting an interview — the only issue that interrogators questioned him about — is a violation of international law,” Lander said when he published the letter. “It comes at a time when senior Israeli officials are trying to delegitimize the participation of Palestinian citizens in Israel’s recent elections.”

Nor do Israel’s problems end with angry Democrats. The wounded Republican establishment lost no time looking a few thousand miles away to find reasons for the collapse of its voter base.

Soon after the election results came in, the vice-president, JD Vance, put “our relationship with Israel” on a short list of reasons for voter fury, and on election day Trump made a last-ditch attempt to woo voters with a pledge to cut off $4bn (£3bn) in annual military aid to Israel.

The announcement caused panic in Israel’s defence establishment. “When the commander of the Israel air force hears something like that, he might slit his wrists,” one official told Channel 12 news. “Where are we going to come up with 15 billion shekels every year, and what does that mean for Israel’s future defence budget?”

Netanyahu only responded to Trump’s electioneering on Friday with an attempt to spin the cut as a joint decision reflecting Israel’s economic strength. It demonstrated a “move from aid to partnership”, his office said in a statement.

Netanyahu has long flaunted his relationship with Trump, his fluent English and experience in the US, presenting himself as the only man with the international standing to guarantee Israel’s security in a hostile world.

After Tuesday’s US election, he looks more like an agent of its destruction to many in Israel. “One thing is clear: we are losing America,” Ben Caspit wrote in Ma’ariv, a daily newspaper.

“This isn’t a process; it isn’t happening in stages; it is happening all at once. It is an avalanche. It is a reverberating collapse of the foundation of Israel’s national defence doctrine. This isn’t a decree of fate. It is a decree of Netanyahu.”

Some advocates for change inside Israel found cause for hope in the Democrats’ victory, if Israel’s opposition can turn their mandate for change into a new government. They won 67 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, but more than a quarter went to Palestinian citizens of Israel, and some of the Jewish Israeli opposition parties have ruled out sitting with them.

US administrations have for too long equated support for Israel with blind support for its government, said Nadav Tamir, a former senior Israeli diplomat in the US who is now executive director of J Street Israel.

That consensus is cracking, but the majority of lawmakers from both parties still see Israel as a key US ally in the Middle East, he wrote in the Times of Israel.

External pressure from those who support its security but see current policy as self-destructive might push the country towards necessary change, including a resolution of the Israel-Palestine conflict.

“Perhaps this will be the paradox of the new [US] Congress,” he wrote. “It will be less willing to define support for Israel as automatic alignment with every policy of its government, but precisely for that reason, it may offer Israel more meaningful support in breaking out of the cycle of wars and building a future of security and prosperity.”

articles.title: In Sudafrica l’Anc non fa più presa nelle città
articles.summary: I sudafricani hanno votato per le amministrative con in mente i problemi causati dalla cattiva gestione dei servizi pubblici. Per l’African national congress il verdetto è stato duro
articles.preview: Il 4 novembre, mentre il resto del mondo era concentrato sui risultati delle elezioni di metà mandato negli Stati Uniti, i sudafricani sono andati alle urne per rinnovare più di 10.500 consigli municipali, tra cui quelli delle otto città metropolitane, che comprendono centri importanti come Pretoria, Johannesburg, Città del Capo, Durban e Bloemfontein. La legge sudafricana non prevede l’elezione diretta del sindaco, che viene scelto dal nuovo consiglio locale entro 14 giorni dal voto.
articles.body:
Il 4 novembre, mentre il resto del mondo era concentrato sui risultati delle elezioni di metà mandato negli Stati Uniti, i sudafricani sono andati alle urne per rinnovare più di 10.500 consigli municipali, tra cui quelli delle otto città metropolitane, che comprendono centri importanti come Pretoria, Johannesburg, Città del Capo, Durban e Bloemfontein.

La legge sudafricana non prevede l’elezione diretta del sindaco, che viene scelto dal nuovo consiglio locale entro 14 giorni dal voto. Quindi le preferenze di elettori ed elettrici – la cui affluenza alle urne è stata del al 54,5 per cento, in crescita rispetto al 2021 – non si rivolgono a singoli candidati, ma hanno anche un importante valore di termometro politico, in particolare sull’operato dell’African national congress (Anc), il partito nato dal movimento di liberazione guidato da Nelson Mandela, che è al potere dalla fine dell’apartheid, nel 1994.

Come previsto prima del voto, il verdetto è stato spietato. Già dai risultati parziali delle elezioni amministrative è apparso chiaramente che il partito del presidente Cyril Ramaphosa ha perso gran parte di quel consenso e di quella legittimità che gli avevano permesso di governare indisturbato per trent’anni. E li ha persi a causa dei pessimi servizi pubblici erogati alla popolazione, a cominciare dalla distribuzione dell’acqua potabile.

Un’immagine del vignettista Zapiro riassume bene la situazione: dalla torre per le telecomunicazioni, simbolo di Johannesburg, sporge un rubinetto – gestito dall’Anc – da cui esce un’unica goccia d’acqua, che cade nel secchio vuoto dei voti per il partito. Sullo sfondo, alcune persone fanno la fila per prendere l’acqua da un camion cisterna. “È a secco!”, commenta un funzionario vestito con i colori del partito. “Chissà come mai…”, risponde una signora.

Uno dei temi principali della campagna elettorale è stato proprio l’accesso all’acqua potabile, uno dei problemi più gravi per le popolazioni urbane del Sudafrica, in un contesto generale di dissesto finanziario, infrastrutture carenti o in stato di abbandono, interruzioni di corrente elettrica e cattiva gestione della raccolta dei rifiuti.

Secondo il sito sudafricano Groundup, in più della metà delle città che si occupano del trattamento dell’acqua la qualità di quest’ultima è insoddisfacente, se non pessima. E, anche se la qualità dell’acqua è buona, le amministrazioni locali non sono sempre in grado di distribuirla efficacemente, a causa delle perdite nella rete idrica. Il risultato è che in alcune aree i residenti restano senz’acqua corrente per giorni. Secondo Groundup la situazione di oggi è leggermente migliore rispetto ai tempi della presidenza di Jacob Zuma (2009-2018), nota come il “decennio perduto” a causa dei livelli altissimi di corruzione e di appropriazione indebita delle risorse pubbliche. Ma c’è ancora molto lavoro da fare.

L’Anc ne ha pagato il conto. Il declino non è recente, come mostra questa mappa: se nel 2004 aveva ottenuto quasi il 70 per cento dei voti a livello nazionale, alle amministrative del 2021 il partito era sceso per la prima volta sotto il 50 per cento. Alle politiche del 2024 aveva registrato poco più del 40 per cento dei voti a suo favore ed era stato costretto per la prima volta a formare un governo di unità nazionale con altri nove partiti, tra cui la Democratic alliance (Da), il partito di riferimento della minoranza bianca. Dal suo feudo di Città del Capo, la Da, guidata da Helen Zille, 75 anni, ha cominciato a fare presa anche nel resto del paese, tanto che oggi rischia di strappare all’Anc il controllo di Pretoria e di Johannesburg, il motore economico del paese.

Zille, che in passato è stata criticata per le sue posizioni sulla questione razziale, si è proposta come candidata sindaca di Joburg, scommettendo sul fatto che i cittadini siano più interessati a temi come la qualità della vita e dei servizi, che alla sua appartenenza razziale. E il voto potrebbe non darle torto. Con queste elezioni l’Anc è diventato un “partito di campagna”, scrive il commentatore del Financial Times David Pilling.

La formazione è ancora radicata nelle zone rurali, ma è in caduta libera nelle grandi città, dove si fanno sentire di più i disservizi e gli altri problemi che affliggono il paese, come l’insicurezza dovuta alla criminalità e alla violenza politica (solo all’avvicinarsi di queste elezioni sono stati registrati venti casi di omicidi a sfondo politico). Se a livello nazionale i risultati preliminari danno l’Anc al 32 per cento, con la Da al 24 per cento, in città come Johannesburg e Pretoria il partito di Zille è decisamente in testa. A Durban, il più grande porto del paese, invece è andato forte il partito uMkhonto we Sizwe (Mk), dell’ex presidente Zuma, la Da è seconda e l’Anc terzo.

Si aprirà presto una fase di intense trattative per formare coalizioni stabili in grado di governare le grandi città del paese. L’Anc e la Da sono già partner nel governo nazionale dal 2024, e finora la loro alleanza ha resistito nonostante le molte divergenze. “Molti elettori sudafricani stanno cominciando a non votare più in base a criteri razziali ed etnici… per scegliere in base alla competenza” dei candidati, nota il commentatore sudafricano William Gumede sul Mail & Guardian. La speranza è che i vincitori di queste elezioni amministrative si dimostrino all’altezza.

Questo testo è tratto dalla newsletter Africana.

articles.title: Cina, dalla bolla immobiliare alla bolla delle auto
articles.summary: Quest’anno nel paese i profitti del settore sono crollati. Lo stato continua a sovvenzionare aziende in perdita, creando una situazione potenzialmente esplosiva

articles.body:
A settembre le case automobilistiche cinesi hanno registrato una diminuzione dei profitti pari al 68 per cento rispetto allo stesso periodo di un anno fa. Il calo riguarda quasi tutti i maggiori produttori: nel terzo trimestre del 2026 la Saic Motor, la leader di mercato, ha registrato utili in discesa del 76,7 per cento; la Chongqing Changan Automobile ha perso 760 milioni di yuan (poco più di cento milioni di euro); la Anhui Jianghuai Automobile Group ha avuto una perdita netta di 1,1 miliardi di yuan nei primi nove mesi del 2026; la Seres Group ha registrato un utile netto di 1,4 miliardi di yuan nel terzo trimestre di quest’anno, ma se si escludono le voci non legate alla normale attività dell’azienda risulta una perdita di 1,4 miliardi di yuan. I rappresentanti del settore automobilistico cinese hanno dichiarato che il 2026 potrebbe chiudersi con 18,5 milioni di veicoli venduti, il dato peggiore dal 2014.

Le cause sono l’aumento dei costi e il crollo della domanda interna. Un fatto poco sorprendente in un paese dove la popolazione invecchia costantemente e in generale consuma poco (i consumi cinesi corrispondono al 40 per cento del pil, contro il 70 per cento degli Stati Uniti), i trasporti pubblici sono abbastanza efficienti e i taxi a guida autonoma sono ormai una realtà in molti centri urbani. Per questo sul più grande mercato automobilistico del mondo, spiega il sito Caixin Global, è in corso da tempo una brutale corsa al ribasso dei prezzi tra le numerosissime aziende del settore, una selezione darwiniana che sta mettendo in ginocchio molte di loro.

La posta in gioco

Il dato suscita non pochi interrogativi: com’è possibile che il settore sia in calo mentre il resto del mondo – l’Europa innanzitutto, basta pensare ai guai della Volkswagen – è letteralmente inondato dai veicoli cinesi? La risposta più immediata è che in Cina si è creata una bolla simile a quella che negli scorsi anni ha devastato il settore immobiliare: c’è un forte eccesso di produzione che finora è stato ampiamente assorbito attraverso le esportazioni; ma tutto questo potrebbe non bastare più. Com’è successo nel caso dell’immobiliare, inoltre, non sarà facile assorbire quest’altra bolla, soprattutto perché anche in questo caso, oltre ad aziende e posti di lavoro, è in gioco la stabilità di molti enti locali cinesi, profondamente coinvolti nello sviluppo del settore automobilistico.

Un interessante articolo del Wall Street Journal racconta il caso della Skyworth Auto, un’azienda che nel 2021 sosteneva di poter produrre centomila auto elettriche all’anno, ma che nei primi nove mesi del 2026 ha venduto appena 660 vetture. La Skyworth oggi resta in vita grazie agli aiuti del distretto di Nanchino, che possiede il 5 per cento del suo capitale. Un anno fa, scrive il quotidiano statunitense, sul sito web dell’amministrazione di Nanchino si leggeva che la Skyworth aveva ricevuto “il sostegno completo di tutti i dipartimenti governativi” e che l’aiuto dell’amministrazione aveva permesso di superare “gli ostacoli incontrati dall’azienda nel suo sviluppo”.

La Skyworth non è un’eccezione. Per anni gli enti locali cinesi hanno stretto alleanze con i privati per investire nel settore automobilistico: ogni città puntava sul “campione locale” sperando di diventare la Detroit cinese. Il fenomeno si è accentuato con l’arrivo dell’auto elettrica: alla fine del 2025 le aziende cinesi di auto elettriche che vendevano almeno un modello erano 143. La Nio, azienda pioniere del settore oggi quotata alla borsa di Wall street, stava per dichiarare insolvenza prima che nel 2020 l’amministrazione comunale di Hefei la salvasse con un investimento di quasi settecento milioni di dollari. La città voleva costruire intorno alla Nio un parco industriale dedicato alle auto elettriche con l’obiettivo di dare lavoro a migliaia di persone.

La proliferazione di accordi simili, unita al credito facile concesso dalle banche, ha fatto nascere un settore abnorme in grado di fabbricare 63 milioni di auto all’anno, più del triplo di quelle che nel 2026 dovrebbero essere comprate dai cinesi. Il resto finisce all’estero, su un mercato globale che ogni anno assorbe circa 85 milioni di auto (settanta se si escludono gli Stati Uniti, un mercato praticamente inaccessibile ai cinesi).

Di fronte al calo della domanda interna, alle aziende cinesi restano due scelte, aggiunge il Wall Street Journal: da un lato riducono i prezzi per accaparrarsi una fetta del mercato interno (dall’inizio del 2023 i prezzi dei veicoli cinesi sono diminuiti di quasi il 20 per cento); dall’altro puntano sulle esportazioni (quest’anno la Cina dovrebbe vendere all’estero dodici milioni di auto, all’inizio del decennio in corso le vendite annuali si aggiravano sul milione), sfruttando tra l’altro uno yuan perennemente svalutato da Pechino.

Ora la Cina comincia ad accorgersi che questa strategia non può continuare a lungo: all’interno i prezzi non possono scendere ulteriormente; all’estero gli altri paesi cominciano a reagire all’ondata di auto cinesi, che sta mettendo in ginocchio le loro aziende. Insomma, addossare al resto del mondo i punti deboli della propria economia non è la soluzione.

Il problema è che il presidente Xi Jinping non sembra avere il pieno controllo della situazione, soprattutto perché molte amministrazioni locali invischiate nel settore automobilistico non hanno intenzione di staccare la spina alle aziende, sia perché temono di perdere tanti posti di lavoro sia perché vedrebbero ridursi le loro entrate fiscali, danneggiando ulteriormente finanze già messe a dura prova dall’esplosione della bolla immobiliare.

La spirale del debito

La Cina, lanciata da Xi Jinping in grandiosi progetti legati alle tecnologie militari e civili più avanzate (dai pannelli solari all’intelligenza artificiale), è finita in una pericolosa spirale del debito: nel 2025 i prestiti concessi a settori non finanziari – grandi conglomerati industriali, enti pubblici e famiglie – hanno raggiunto il 300 per cento del pil nazionale, 60 punti percentuali in più rispetto alla fine del 2019 e 43mila miliardi di dollari in più del 2012, cioè da quando Xi è arrivato al potere. Molto di questo denaro è stato buttato prima in immobili che oggi non vuole nessuno e poi in fabbriche che perdono soldi perché non trovano abbastanza acquirenti e non possono più di tanto abbassare i prezzi o decurtare i salari degli operai.

L’enorme mole di debiti e attività in perdita forse non provocherà una crisi finanziaria in un paese come la Cina, ma di sicuro ne sta indebolendo l’economia. Le prospettive rosee suscitate dalla straordinaria crescita degli ultimi decenni stanno lasciando il posto al pessimismo: quello di molti giovani, che fanno fatica a trovare occupazioni adeguate alle loro competenze; e quello di molti lavoratori che, tagliati fuori dall’automazione, ormai si riciclano nel mondo precario della gig economy (quest’anno il numero dei cosiddetti gig worker cinesi dovrebbe arrivare a 320 milioni, contro i 280 milioni del 2025).

Xi forse pensa che tutto si possa risolvere quando la Cina si affermerà come una potenza globale del livello degli Stati Uniti, se non superiore a loro. Anche per questo continua a ignorare gli appelli di molti economisti – cinesi e non – che consigliano di far crescere i consumi interni: questa svolta darebbe respiro sia alle aziende in cerca di clienti sia ai lavoratori, oltre a creare nuove entrate per lo stato e le amministrazioni locali; ne sarebbero felici anche gli altri paesi, alle prese con l’ondata di esportazioni cinesi.

Tuttavia, aumentare i consumi interni ridurrebbe la presa di Pechino sull’economia nazionale e distoglierebbe capitali da settori che Xi giudica strategici. Intanto, per aiutare le finanze pubbliche Pechino ha lanciato una vasta campagna contro l’evasione e l’elusione fiscale dei ricchi cinesi. Ma come osservano gli economisti Navneeraj Sharma e Arvind Subramanian, a questo punto “è probabile che si verifichi un lento declino caratterizzato da una crescita anemica, un crescente malcontento e un deterioramento dei servizi”. Comunque sufficiente per avere ripercussioni sull’intera economia globale.

Questo testo è tratto dalla newsletter Economica.

articles.title: L'Ucraina al buio per i raid. Allarme di Berlino sui Patriot
articles.summary: Pistorius: per ora non riusciamo a darne altri. Zelensky, così Mosca si prepara a colloqui
articles.preview: In attesa del "big, beautiful agreement" sull'Ucraina evocato da Donald Trump e del trilaterale di Abu Dhabi di martedì e mercoledì prossimi, l'Ucraina resta sempre più al buio e al freddo sotto i massicci bombardamenti russi. Con il ferale annuncio del ministro della Difesa tedesco, Boris Pistorius, che Berlino non è più in grado, al momento, di fornire i Patriot a Kiev per non sguarnire i propri arsenali.
articles.body:
In attesa del "big, beautiful agreement" sull'Ucraina evocato da Donald Trump e del trilaterale di Abu Dhabi di martedì e mercoledì prossimi, l'Ucraina resta sempre più al buio e al freddo sotto i massicci bombardamenti russi. Con il ferale annuncio del ministro della Difesa tedesco, Boris Pistorius, che Berlino non è più in grado, al momento, di fornire i Patriot a Kiev per non sguarnire i propri arsenali. Le forze russe hanno colpito duramente le infrastrutture energetiche intorno alla capitale ucraina con missili e droni durante la notte, mettendo sotto forte pressione le forniture elettriche e i sistemi di riscaldamento di Kiev, mentre le temperature si avvicinavano allo zero. Colpito e danneggiato anche il Ponte Nord, che attraversa il fiume Dnipro. Gli attacchi contro gli impianti energetici situati fuori Kiev, compresi i sistemi che trasportano l'elettricità da due centrali nucleari verso la capitale e le regioni centrali dell'Ucraina, hanno provocato gravi danni, ha riferito il ministero dell' Energia. "La capitale sta affrontando gravi difficoltà nelle forniture di elettricità, acqua e riscaldamento", ha dichiarato il presidente Volodymyr Zelensky su X, aggiungendo che anche le sottostazioni elettriche di altre cinque regioni sono state colpite. Almeno due persone sono rimaste uccise e circa una dozzina sono state ferite negli attacchi notturni, che hanno provocato danni ad abitazioni, attività commerciali, edifici residenziali e non, compreso un asilo. "La Russia si prepara ai colloqui trilaterali lanciandoci missili balistici", ha denunciato Zelensky, accusando Mosca di intensificare gli attacchi "per esercitare pressione" in vista della ripresa dei negoziati negli Emirati Arabi. Il leader di Kiev ha riferito che negli ultimi raid i russi hanno utilizzato 36 missili balistici, tra cui gli KN-23 prodotti e forniti dalla Corea del Nord, e 172 droni. Mosca ha intensificato gli attacchi aerei contro l'Ucraina perché la propria offensiva terrestre è rimasta sostanzialmente bloccata e Kiev è a corto di sistemi di difesa aerea. Da Berlino è arrivata una doccia fredda: in un'intervista al Berliner Morgenpost, Pistorius ha ammesso che "al momento non possiamo fare di più" sui Patriot, osservando che altri Paesi "hanno fatto significativamente meno" e auspicando un maggiore impegno da parte dei Paesi partner. "Dobbiamo affrontare la questione con estrema serietà in occasione della prossima riunione del Gruppo di contatto per l'Ucraina, prevista per la metà di novembre", ha avvisato.

Nel frattempo, tutti gli occhi sono puntati sul trilaterale di Abu Dhabi, dove il Cremlino ha preannunciato una delegazione folta e qualificata, con diplomatici e militari di alto rango, tra cui, per la prima volta, il viceministro degli Esteri Sergei Ryabkov, insieme a Yuri Zhigarlovsky, alto ufficiale dello Stato Maggiore generale russo. Ci saranno anche il viceministro degli Esteri Mikhail Galuzin e il capo dell'intelligence militare russa Igor Kostyukov, già presenti in precedenti missioni negoziali. A guidarla sarà lo storico Vladimir Medinsky, consigliere del Cremlino. Ma il vero emissario dello zar sembra restare Kirill Dmitriev, che Trump ha ricevuto alla Casa Bianca giovedì scorso, prima di annunciare che "sarà un grande accordo", che "coinvolgerà qualcosa di più dell'Ucraina e potrei persino dire che potrebbe riguardare tutta l'Europa". "Stiamo facendo molti progressi con la Russia e l'Ucraina", ha assicurato venerdì, sottolineando di aver avuto nello stesso giorno delle telefonate e di avere degli incontri in programma lunedì e martedì al riguardo. Ma Ucraina ed Europa sembrano non saperne nulla.

articles.title: Attacco mirato a Qeshm, ma gli Usa sono spaccati sull'Iran
articles.summary: Nell'amministrazione è scontro fra le varie correnti. Vance in prima fila per un accordo
articles.preview: Un attacco mirato a Qeshm di qualche minuto per mostrare i muscoli e far vedere che gli Stati Uniti non mollano la presa. L'azione decisa maschera però l'alta tensione all'interno dell'amministrazione Trump su come procedere nel conflitto, il principale responsabile della scottante sconfitta dei repubblicani alle elezioni di metà mandato. articles.body: Un attacco mirato a Qeshm di qualche minuto per mostrare i muscoli e far vedere che gli Stati Uniti non mollano la presa. L'azione decisa maschera però l'alta tensione all'interno dell'amministrazione Trump su come procedere nel conflitto, il principale responsabile della scottante sconfitta dei repubblicani alle elezioni di metà mandato. Trump è tirato per la giacchetta e sotto pressione dalle diverse correnti che si stanno scontrando alla Casa Bianca mentre cerca di decidere se tornare ad attaccare oppure privilegiare la via diplomatica. "Dobbiamo decidere. Preferirei non distruggere il resto del paese se possibile, ma forse dovremmo farlo. Lo saprete presto", ha detto Trump dopo le midterm confermando di non aver ancora sciolto le riserve. Il commander-in-chief ha da un lato il capo del Pentagono Pete Hegseth e il numero uno dello Us Central Command Brad Cooper che spingono per una escalation, appoggiati anche dal premier israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu. Dall'altro i segretari di stato e del Tesoro, Marco Rubio e Scott Bessent, che premono per ulteriori sanzioni e la continuazione del blocco americano nel Golfo così da soffocare e piegare l'Iran. Appoggiato da Trump, Bessent ha parlato di recente dell'Iran anche con la Cina chiedendo - riporta il Washington Post - di usare la sua influenza su Teheran per mettere fine al conflitto. In prima fila per trovare una soluzione c'è JD Vance: con il 2028 in vista, il vicepresidente è in costante contatto con i mediatori del Qatar e del Pakistan, che stanno discutendo la possibilità di un incontro a livello tecnico fra gli Stati Uniti e l'Iran nei prossimi giorni. Per Vance chiudere la guerra sarebbe un'occasione per rilanciare la sua candidatura alle presidenziali, che appare in pericolo dopo l'onda blu emersa dalle midterm. Anche la spinta di Rubio a una soluzione diplomatica appare inquadrata in un'ottica di corsa alla Casa Bianca. Pur non essendo stato direttamente coinvolto nelle trattative con l'Iran, Rubio è il segretario di Stato (oltre che consigliere per la sicurezza nazionale), un ruolo che difficilmente lo mette al riparo per le critiche ad un conflitto bocciato dagli americani. Le trattative proseguono dietro le quinte e, secondo indiscrezioni riportate dal Wall Street Journal, l'accordo in discussione prevede di ridurre i tempi delle trattative preliminari da 60 giorni - la durata prevista dal memorandum di giugno - a due giorni, per poi passare immediatamente ai negoziati sul nucleare. Questa opzione aprirebbe al presidente una via di uscita per iniziare a porre fine al conflitto. Non è chiaro però se l'Iran accetterà tale ipotesi. Come molti presidenti 'anatra zoppa', anche Trump è probabile che dedicherà più tempo alla politica estera, area in cui il suo potere è meno limitato dal Congresso. Questo fa sì che la guerra in Iran e quella in Ucraina saranno le sue priorità, alle quali però - affermano gli osservatori - deve avvicinarsi consapevole di essere politicamente più debole. L'esito del voto appare infatti in grado di rafforzare l'Ucraina, l'Europa e forse l'Iran. La Russia invece potrebbe perdere terreno perchè le capacità di Trump di arrivare a un accordo favorevole a Vladimir Putin sono ora più ridotte.

articles.body:
It happened in a region of the country known to have drug trafficking activity.

A Guatemalan lawmaker and three police officers have been killed in an armed attack, according to the country’s authorities.

The attack on Friday targeted Congressman Julio Portillo, who was in the town of Rio Hondo, in the eastern Zacapa department, which is known for drug trafficking activity.

Portillo was initially taken to a hospital with serious injuries. His death was later confirmed by the National Unity of Hope party, or UNE, to which he belonged.

“President Luis Contreras, members of the Board of Directors and lawmakers mourn the tragic passing of Congressman Julio Cesar Portillo Paz, representative of the Zacapa district,” Guatemala’s Congress posted late Friday on X.

President Bernardo Arevalo said the three National Civil Police officers killed in the attack had died in the line of duty and instructed security forces to cooperate with prosecutors investigating the killings.

Authorities have not disclosed a motive for the attack or identified who was responsible.

The Lorenzana family cartel, which has links to Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel, controls the drug trade in Zacapa.

Portillo won his seat in 2023 for the opposition party Cabal, but has since switched to the National Unity of Hope party led by former First Lady Sandra Torres.

She is expected to run for president in Guatemala’s elections next year.

The killings come about three weeks after former anticorruption prosecutor Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa was shot dead in Guatemala City, a case that heightened concerns about organised crime’s influence and the possible return of politically motivated assassinations.

Authorities have not established a connection between the two attacks.

articles.title: Iran’s IRGC says building underground sites for weapons production, storage
articles.summary: IRGC says underground military complexes allow missile production to continue even under heavy bombardment.
articles.preview: IRGC says underground military complexes allow missile production to continue even under heavy bombardment. Iran is building underground military complexes able to sustain weapons production and storage even under heavy bombardment, according to the country’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC). IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi made a series of announcements on Saturday about the military’s capabilities during a news conference in Tehran, Iranian media reported.
articles.body:
IRGC says underground military complexes allow missile production to continue even under heavy bombardment.

Iran is building underground military complexes able to sustain weapons production and storage even under heavy bombardment, according to the country’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC).

IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi made a series of announcements on Saturday about the military’s capabilities during a news conference in Tehran, Iranian media reported.

Among the achievements listed were an “underground missile city” set to be unveiled, the semi-official Tasnim news agency reported.

Mohebbi said the IRGC had rapidly transferred its missile and drone production lines from the surface to underground facilities. This allows Iran to continue producing missiles while its adversaries assumed its stockpiles were dwindling, he explained.

The spokesperson also outlined advances in stealth technology. He maintained that such improvements had allowed Iran’s missiles and drones to pierce air defence systems and accurately strike targets during previous rounds of fighting with the United States and Israel.

“Today, every weapon used by the IRGC Aerospace Force is manufactured using homegrown knowledge and expertise. Moreover, our products are not even derived from reverse-engineering captured enemy war material,” Iran’s IRNA news agency quoted Mohebbi as saying.

A recent report by US newspaper, The Wall Street Journal, shows that Iran caused billions of dollars in damage to US bases throughout the Middle East during previous rounds of fighting.

Meanwhile, a separate report by the Reuters news agency found that Iran had successfully targeted Gulf infrastructure on at least 135 occasions during the same period, causing billions of dollars in damage and lost revenues.

Mohebbi also warned on Saturday that restrictions on the range of Iranian missiles had been lifted. The warning follows a statement from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who said that there would be “no geographical limits” to Iran’s response if it were attacked again by the US and Israel.

The US-Israeli war on Iran was launched on February 28, prompting Tehran to close the Strait of Hormuz and triggering a global energy crisis. Mediation efforts have stepped up recently, as regional countries hope to bring the war to an end.

On Friday, President Donald Trump said the US military launched limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, while also claiming Washington had made “a lot of progress” in talks with Iran.

Tehran has repeatedly warned that it will target Gulf energy infrastructure if the fighting resumes. Such attacks would likely push energy prices even higher.

Meanwhile, Washington has also imposed additional sanctions on Iran as it seeks to force Tehran to concede to its demands. The restrictions have further strained the country’s economy, forcing Iran to adopt new trade routes.

On Saturday, US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced it was establishing a new task force that will support ongoing US efforts to prevent Iran from using land routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials.

The US has also imposed a naval blockade on Iran to prevent it from exporting oil.

articles.title: US midterms: Not even Trump's Israel aid stunt could rescue the Republicans
articles.summary: US midterms: Not even Trump's Israel aid stunt could rescue the Republicans Submitted by Mohamad Elmasry on Thu, 11/05/2026 - 18:21 Washington's support for its ally has become an electoral liability, but ending the annual funding package could pave the way for deeper military cooperation A Democratic campaign sign showing a mugshot of US President Donald Trump lies on the ground outside a polling station in Indianapolis during the midterm election, on 3 November (USA Today Network via Reuters) Off There is nothing particularly unusual about an election stunt. Politicians routinely perform them. Rarely, though, is a stunt as obvious as the one US President Donald Trump pulled on 3 November, Election Day, when he announced that America would, at year's end, stop providing $4bn in annual military aid to Israel . Trump had clearly read the room, and the polls. For all his public disdain for polls he claims are "fake" or "rigged", the president understands their political significance. Polling data suggests that American voters are increasingly uncomfortable contributing their tax dollars to Israel's military, particularly as costs rise in the US and Americans struggle to afford basic necessities . An August Marquette Law School poll , for example, found that 52 percent of American adults believe Washington provides Israel with too much military aid. Only 16 percent said it provides too little. Even among Republicans under 30, 54 percent said Washington gives Israel too much. Appearing on Fox & Friends that morning, Trump asked why Republicans should "suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed", a reference to Abdul El-Sayed, who hours later would become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Funding for Israel, Trump said , had become "a bad talking point" for Republicans. The admission was remarkable, and it demonstrated, perhaps more clearly than anything else, the extent to which a mainstay of American foreign policy has turned into an electoral liability. Trump's funding cut declaration should be seen for what it was: a desperate, last-ditch attempt to rescue the sinking Republican midterm ship, a political life jacket thrown to Republican candidates running for governorships, the Senate and the House of Representatives. It did not work. The election results look less like a blue wave than a blue tsunami . Democrats gained control of both chambers of Congress, flipping at least seven Republican-held Senate seats and winning important governorships, including in Texas, where a Democrat will govern for the first time in more than three decades. Why the stunt failed Why did Trump's bold attempt to save the midterms for Republicans fail so miserably? There are at least two reasons. First, the midterms were not simply a referendum on Israel. An announcement about aid to Israel, even a significant one, was never going to erase broader American concerns about the economy, the war on Iran , the state of democracy, immigration policy, racism and other issues, some of which overlap. Second, and perhaps more importantly, many Americans likely recognised that Trump's announcement was nothing more than a stunt. Almost as soon as Trump made his declaration, scholars, journalists, activists, and political commentators expressed doubts about various aspects of the supposed aid cut. Academic Marc Owen Jones said only "gullible" people would believe Trump's announcement. The annual aid package represents only a relatively small part of Washington's overall military support for Israel The journalist Glenn Greenwald noted that the US provides Israel with significantly more than $4bn in annual military aid. The commentator Ana Kasparian suggested that a new provision in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) is moving Israel's military into more of a direct partnership with the US military. articles.summary: ‘We do not want to die from the cold’: Gaza families struggle as rain floods shelters Submitted by Ahmed Dremly on Sat, 11/07/2026 - 12:48 With tarpaulins failing and damaged buildings at risk of collapse, families say they have nowhere safe to escape the rain and cold A woman walks through rainwater near tents sheltering displaced Palestinians after heavy rainfall in Khan Younis, southern Gaza Strip, 26 March 2026 (Bashar Taleb/AFP) Off Mansour al-Sakni, 33, watched helplessly as rainwater flooded the makeshift shelter on the roof of a building in Gaza City's al-Tuffah neighbourhood, where he lives with his wife and four children. The family had replaced their old tarpaulins with new ones just two weeks ago. Sakni had sold two water barrels so they could buy new sheets to keep them dry and sheltered. But when the first winter storm swept across the Gaza Strip, the canopy offered little protection. “We woke up and found ourselves surrounded by water. The children were crying. I did not know what to do, and I started crying too,” Sakni told Middle East Eye. “We stood inside the tarpaulin shelter waiting for the rain to stop so we could try to push the water out of the room.” Sakni lives in a 30 square metre room with tarpaulin walls which have been damaged by the weather. “I sold the two water barrels to buy new tarpaulins to protect my family from the rain and wind, but it was no use. Last night we were again flooded by the rain,” he said. Before the war, Sakni earned a living selling newspapers. Now, he has no steady income and the family relies fully on food given out by the community kitchen, known locally as a takiya. His 10-year-old daughter Jana suffers from bad eyesight. She requires glasses, but Sakni can’t afford to buy any. A friend gave him 200 shekels to buy a pair, he said, but he used the money to purchase wood to reinforce the shelter instead. “We are poor people in Gaza. We want to live. We do not want to die from the bombing or the cold. Enough. Have mercy on us.” Displaced Palestinians try to clear floodwater outside their tents amid heavy rain in Gaza City’s al-Remal neighbourhood, 7 November 2026 (Omar al-Qattaa/AFP) Sakni said he was wounded by shrapnel in 2024 while standing in a queue outside a bakery on al-Nasr Street. The fragment struck his back, he said, and the injury causes him severe pain in cold weather. Heavy rainfall flooded thousands of tents across Gaza on Saturday, leaving displaced families exposed to cold, rising water and the risk of further damage to already weakened buildings. Gaza's Civil Defence agency said it had received about 1,500 distress calls in 10 hours after the rain began early on Saturday. At some shelters, water rose by 30 to 40 centimetres, Al Jazeera reported . Civil Defence spokesperson Mahmoud Basal said: “What we feared has actually happened. A few shelter centres were completely flooded, and everyone inside them has now been forced out into the unknown.” ‘The rain came inside’ For Nasmeh al-Khatib, 26, the storm brought back the fear of losing her home and the uncertainty that has defined life since her husband was killed during the family's displacement in Gaza City in 2024. Khatib lives with her two-year-old daughter, Alina, in her family's home in Mashrou Amer in northern Gaza. Five families are sheltering in the partially destroyed building. The house was struck in October 2025, days before the ceasefire, she said. It once had four floors, but three were destroyed. The families now live on the ground floor, which she fears may also be unsafe. “We have covered the house with tarpaulins, but every time it rains, we are flooded,” Khatib told Middle East Eye. A displaced Palestinian woman heats a pot as children look on outside their tent in Gaza City amid rain and cold winter conditions, 28 December 2025 (Omar al-Qattaa/AFP) She said heavy rain and strong winds battered the building overnight, bringing down the sheets used to cover openings and allowing water to enter. Thunder also frightened the children, who woke believing the sounds were from bombs. “My two-year-old daughter cried throughout the night. She asks me, ‘Mum, why is the rain inside the house and not outside? I don't like the rain'," Khatib said. The family has solar panels, but the electricity repeatedly cut out and returned during the night. She said parts of the walls and floor began giving electric shocks, while lights and phone chargers stopped working. “We do not know what to do. All our belongings are wet. Since morning, we have been trying to seal the holes in the walls and tie the tarpaulins in any way we can,” she said. “We know that everything we are doing is in vain and that when it rains again, we will be flooded once more. We need a solution to this suffering.” Winter crisis The storm has exposed the vulnerability of hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians living in tents, makeshift shelters and buildings damaged during Israel's ongoing genocidal war on Gaza . Gaza's emergency committee said more than one million displaced people face winter-related risks and that the territory needs about 200,000 tents, as well as heating supplies, Al Jazeera reported. ‘Complicit’: World Medical Association criticised for rejecting calls to suspend Israel arian Affairs (Ocha), in a report published on 5 November, said people in Gaza still needed approximately 121,000 tents and 561,000 tarpaulins as of 1 November. It said available stocks included about 2,800 tents and 76,000 tarpaulins, while no emergency shelter kits were available. Ocha said the entry of timber needed for shelter kits continued to be rejected by Israeli authorities. It also warned that restrictions on supplies, delays in approvals and funding shortages could mean some materials would not arrive until the second half of the winter. The Norwegian Refugee Council said on 5 October that Israeli restrictions on the entry of shelter materials and funding shortfalls were likely to leave 1.65 million people facing a fourth winter in worn-out tents and war-damaged buildings. Aid organisations have also warned that many displacement sites are at risk of flooding. Shot in class: Gaza's children return to school under Israeli fire people were living at displacement sites facing medium to high flood risks, including more than 400,000 at high risk. The latest storm also damaged buildings already weakened by bombardment. Gaza's Civil Defence said residents were evacuated from a partially collapsed building in Nuseirat, while two people were injured when a wall collapsed in northern Gaza, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa. Civil Defence officials have said their ability to respond is limited by shortages of equipment and supplies. Raed al-Dahshan, director of Civil Defence in Gaza governorate, told Al Jazeera that the agency did not have “a single tarpaulin or a single tent” to distribute to families affected by the flooding. For families such as Sakni's and Khatib's, the problem is not simply the arrival of winter rain, but the absence of a safe place to shelter from it. “I am tired of this life,” Sakni said. “We want the world to find a solution for us." articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.

Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.

Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.

Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said.

Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.

The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.

The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.

They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN, Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.

In a series of social media posts, Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.

Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.

Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”

Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.

Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

Zelensky wrote on Telegram, external that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".

Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.

"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.

"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."

In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.

The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.

Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.

The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.

She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.

She thanked both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.

Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.

"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.

Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhzhia, with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.

Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.

He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.

"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."

Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.

articles.body:
Qatar, the lead mediator in the US-Iran conflict, is seeking to persuade Tehran to allow UN nuclear weapons inspectors to visit Iran’s bombed nuclear sites, including those housing the country’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

Iran would not be required to make any commitment that the stockpile would be removed from the country, with other options on the table, including reducing the uranium content by down-blending it.

Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of Qatar, spoke to Donald Trump about the proposal, the emir’s office said on Friday without revealing the call’s contents.

The state news agency said the emir “emphasised the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, preventing further escalation in the region”.

Trump is still considering whether to mount a further assault on Iranian nuclear sites, though the credibility of his threats is weaker inside Iran after his vice-president, JD Vance, said the war itself, and not just its cost to American consumers, was critical to the collapse of the Republican vote in the US midterms.

Under the Qatar proposal, the US would immediately lift the naval blockade on Iran in the strait of Hormuz and release a portion of the $8bn (£6bn) of its frozen assets. In return, Iran would agree to visits by International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to its bombed nuclear facilities, based on a previous abandoned agreement that had been reached in Cairo in September 2025.

Iran would open the strait of Hormuz on the second day, via a route it has already negotiated with Oman that they would jointly lodge with the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).

Iran has multiple other preconditions for opening the strait including ending the war in Lebanon, a withdrawal of US forces from the Iranian coastline, a commitment to lift some economic sanctions, and agreement to pay war reparations. The sequencing of these commitments has been at the heart of the mediation.

In the memorandum of understanding, a $300bn reconstruction and development fund was to be set up to help Iran recover economically, but it was never clear exactly how this proposal was to be funded.

Iran, in a triumphalist mood after Trump’s election wipeout, has been wary of allowing the UN nuclear inspectors back into the country, claiming it had lost faith in Rafael Grossi, the head of the inspectorate.

Tehran claims Grossi betrayed his duty to uphold the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, by failing to criticise the US for bombing Iran’s nuclear sites. It fears that material gathered by the inspectors would be handed over as targeting data to the Americans and Israelis.

In the parallel talks on opening the strait, Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, spoke again to Iran about the future of the strait administration including the agreed route, the extent to which the agreement is temporary and the need to register the proposal with the IMO, either as a bilateral agreement or a joint regional proposal.

Oman has a long-term proposal for the administration of the strait compliant with the law of the sea in that shipping companies would be charged only for services, and not tolls.

Amir Hayat Moqaddam, the deputy chair of the Iranian parliament’s national security and foreign policy committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) on Tuesday that ships from four countries – China, India, Qatar and Iraq – were allowed to pass through the strategic waterway.

The exemptions served mutual interests, he said, adding that Iran charged Indian and Chinese vessels transit fees while allowing Qatari ships to pass free of charge. Medicine was received from India, while China provided political support.

It is reported that of the 10.23m barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42% went to China and 13% to India, said Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler.

The navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two “violating” oil tankers attempting to pass through an unauthorised route in the eastern sector of the strait of Hormuz had collided with mines and caught fire.

The IRGC said the two tankers had turned off their navigation and identification systems and that the attempted crossing was with the support of US military forces.

articles.title: El archivo suizo del nazi Mengele: pistas que no llevan a nada y un supuesto espía israelí

articles.body:
Los documentos desclasificados sobre el ‘Ángel de la Muerte’ muestran el interés público por hallar al macabro criminal huido tras la II Guerra Mundial

El 14 de mayo de 1964, a las 15.30, el señor Socker se presenta en el internado Monte Rosa de Montreux (Suiza) sin cita previa. Pide ser recibido por un asunto urgente. Es un tipo “simpático”, de mediana estatura, pelo negro peinado “a la moda”, y con un “excelente alemán”. A sus 33 años, dice ser estudiante en la Universidad de Jerusalén y miembro del Congreso Judío Mundial, pero “arrinconado” por las preguntas sobre su persona, admite ser del “servicio secreto israelí”. Busca al criminal nazi Josef Mengele, cuyo sobrino estudia en el internado suizo. El informe policial sobre el intento de conseguir pistas en torno al paradero del macabro médico del campo de exterminio de Auschwitz, huido tras la II Guerra Mundial, concluye en un apartado de “características generales”, que Socker es un “mal mentiroso”, sin más. El supuesto espía fue despedido con una advertencia policial de no dedicarse a indagar más en Montreaux, según los documentos sobre el incidente, que forman parte de un archivo sobre Mengele del servicio de inteligencia suizo (NBD, en sus siglas en alemán) que no iba a ver la luz hasta 2071.

El dosier, de 217 páginas, ha sido desclasificado recientemente, aunque una parte de los datos están velados con un trazo negro. La ocultación de parte de la información a manos del NDB por supuesta necesidad de proteger fuentes o a su personal ha levantado una polvareda entre historiadores suizos, que exigen ver una versión completa y temen que este caso sea un precedente para futuras censuras.

El interés por el archivo de Mengele partió de una investigación de la historiadora y periodista suiza Regula Bochsler, que seguía la pista de otro nazi y se topó con una negativa al querer consultar el dosier. Otro historiador, Gérard Wettstein, decidió recurrir judicialmente la clasificación de los documentos, sobre los que el NDB finalmente aceptó dar acceso con condiciones que se han traducido en la censura de parte del material.

“Solo el examen del expediente original sin censura permite realizar una evaluación científica e histórica independiente”, ha argumentado en un comunicado Wettstein, que ya ha recurrido esa censura judicialmente. Además, “las tachaduras son de aficionado. Hay datos que en un sitio están velados y en otro se pueden leer. Es inconsistente. Hay incluso nombres de los que se tachan datos que se pueden encontrar en Wikipedia o en un registro mercantil. Es de un diletantismo puro”, critica Bochsler en una conversación telefónica. La Sociedad Suiza de Historiadores, por su parte, ve “muy problemáticas” las tachaduras del expediente y reclama que los profesionales puedan ver el acta completa. El revuelo en torno al archivo ha llevado incluso al copresidente de los socialistas suizos, Cédric Wermuth, a registrar una pregunta parlamentaria al respecto.

El archivo contiene informes variados sobre pistas que no llevan a nada, entre otros documentos, como la ficha de búsqueda por “asesinatos” de Interpol, y un sinfín de recortes de periódicos relacionados con Mengele que reflejan el interés público por la localización del llamado Ángel de la Muerte, apodado así por los sádicos experimentos con personas y asesinatos que llevó a cabo en el campo de concentración. Falleció en 1979 en Brasil tras vivir primero en Argentina y Paraguay, pero sus restos no fueron identificados hasta 1985. Nunca fue juzgado.

La orden internacional de detención de Mengele en 1959, y el secuestro por agentes israelíes del nazi Adolf Eichmann en Argentina al año siguiente, mantuvieron viva la atracción por la huida del Ángel de la Muerte. También en Suiza, donde disfrutó tranquilamente de unas vacaciones de esquí con su hijo en 1956, como demostraron fotografías publicadas por el semanario alemán Bunte años después.

Pero el archivo suizo solo incluye recortes de prensa sobre este asunto y, en general, no refleja que las autoridades tomaran la iniciativa de buscar a Mengele. “No fueron proactivos, se limitaron a comprobar datos, no lo buscaban activamente”, afirma Bochsler.

Los documentos informan básicamente de avisos de supuesto avistamiento del criminal que se fueron descartando. Así, una mujer creyó haber visto al nazi en 1980 o 1981 ―aunque no se supiera entonces, ya estaba muerto― en una granja aislada de Irlanda, trabajando como apicultor bajo el nombre de Braendle, y a principios de los años sesenta se siguieron indicios sobre un informante que lo situaba en Ascona con el nombre de doctor Merk y en Ginebra con el supuesto alias de Gregori. De esta época datan también peticiones de búsqueda de las autoridades alemanas, que transmiten la posibilidad de que esté en Brasil o Suiza, y averiguaciones sobre los movimientos del sobrino (y también hijastro) de Mengele en Montreaux, donde se dice que no recibe visitas y se verifican sus movimientos en vacaciones hasta descartar un encuentro con el criminal nazi.

El dosier no responde, sin embargo, a las dudas en torno a la actuación de las autoridades suizas en la primavera de 1961, cuando su segunda esposa y viuda de su hermano, Marta Mengele, alquiló un piso en una localidad cercana al aeropuerto de Zúrich y fue brevemente vigilada por si aparecía el nazi tras la denuncia de un periodista alemán que afirmó haber visto en su balcón a un hombre que podía ser el criminal buscado. La mujer se marchó una mañana en coche acompañada por un hombre sin que nadie los detuviera.

Detalles sobre lo ocurrido no forman parte de este archivo ―hay informes policiales al respecto en otro organismo―, pero sí el interrogatorio a Marta Mengele cuando pidió un permiso de residencia y la decisión de denegárselo. Las propias autoridades de Zúrich cuestionaron su estancia en Kloten, una localidad anodina pero muy cerca del aeropuerto. ¿Por qué no vivir en Montreux, cerca del internado de su hijo? Ella contestó que no hablaba francés. La resolución también constata que pese a sostener que lleva dos años sin contacto con Mengele, tiene intención de volver con él y “no ha hecho nada para distanciarse oficialmente de las opiniones y los actos de su marido”, lo que es contrario al “interés público del país”. La mujer tuvo que abandonar Suiza y se instaló en Merano (Italia); su hijo regresó a Alemania tras terminar sus estudios en el país.

articles.body:
Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.”

Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February.

In an exchange with reporters on Friday, Trump said “they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five”.

The US military had previously reported carrying out what it described as “defensive” strikes on Monday, when explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.

Friday’s strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US.

The electoral setback was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s execution of the Iran war and elevated fuel prices – a byproduct of the war that has affected nearly every part of the global economy.

In the days since, Trump has vacillated between threatening to “destroy” Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near.

Differences with Iran about its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.

US Central Command, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, announced in a post on X late Friday that the US was offering “a reward of up to $20m and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”.

The post included a link to the state department’s Rewards for Justice program.

Trump noted earlier Friday in an exchange with reporters that mediators’ discussions with Iran continue.

“We are talking to Iran. We have been,” said Trump.

A flurry of diplomatic phone calls in recent days between leaders in the Gulf and beyond has been aimed at easing tensions in the region. Concerns have mounted over the possibility that Trump could still order the US military to carry out new strikes against Iran.

US defense secretary Pete Hegseth spoke on Friday with his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, about developments, according to the Qatari government. Qatar has been mediating between the US and Iran to end the war.

The Qatari government announced the call between the countries’ defence officials after confirming earlier that Trump and Qatar’s emir had a separate call to discuss efforts to de-escalate tensions.

The telephone call between Trump and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani focused on international efforts to end tensions, according to a statement from the Qatari ruler’s media office.

With the Associated Press

European officials are also adamant that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s pre-war demands that would effectively roll back NATO’s presence in Eastern Europe are still unacceptable, said the people, who asked not to be identified to discuss private deliberations.

articles.summary: The United Nations on Friday said about 15.4 million people who have fled conflict in Sudan need emergency shelter and essential household items, but humanitarian organisations are facing funding shortages.

articles.body:
Sudan

Millions of people who have fled devastating conflict in Sudan face being left without shelter, the United Nations warned Friday.

After more than three years of civil war, the UN estimates that 15.4 million people need emergency shelter and essential household items.

But UN agencies said they had only been able to target 10% of those in need because of funding shortages.

And out of those, "we could reach only 900,000 people," said Mohamed Refaat, the International Organization for Migration's (IOM) chief of mission in Sudan.

The war raging since April 2023 between the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and the regular army has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate, and has triggered the world's largest hunger and displacement crises.

Around 8.6 million people remain displaced within the country, millions have fled across borders and millions more have returned home — often finding houses, infrastructure and essential services damaged or destroyed.

Since the start of the year, Refaat said the UN agency had distributed more than 40,000 tents.

"But our warehouses are completely empty now," he told reporters in Geneva, speaking from Khartoum.

"We could soon reach a point where families desperately need shelter but there is simply nothing left."

In a joint statement, UNHCR and IOM said for those returning home getting help to find shelter "is often the first step towards rebuilding their lives".

But only one third of the $179 million needed this year to provide shelter has so far been funded, Abubakarr Jalloh, UNHCR's deputy representative in Sudan, told reporters.

Three in four internally displaced people in Sudan are women and children, Jalloh said, adding that El Niño-related weather conditions have made people more vulnerable because of significantly below-average rainfall across Sudan this year.

This has affected harvests in Darfur, Kordofan and other areas already devastated by ongoing fighting. Although food prices would normally ease after the harvest season, prices remain “painfully high,” the UNHCR official said.

“For a family that has lost everything, every Sudanese pound spent on food is money that cannot be spent on a blanket or on materials needed for safe shelter,” Jalloh stressed.

The agencies said less than half of the $2.9 billion needed for the overall humanitarian aid plan for Sudan had been funded.

articles.body:
Water

Children around the world are at greater risk from disease, malnutrition and violence due to a sharp rise in attacks on water and sanitation systems. Now UNICEF is calling on conflict parties, governments and humanitarian actors to treat those systems as life-saving civilian infrastructure.

According to a new report from the UN Children's Agency, attacks that damaged or destroyed water and sanitation systems in conflict rose threefold between 2021 and 2025.

That deprives children of safe drinking water and exposes them to disease from poor sanitation. The report also documents how children in Gaza have been killed or injured while queuing for water.

Longer more dangerous journeys also raise their risk of sexual violence and take time away from school.

Efforts need to be made to guarantee humanitarian access so that water and energy supplies keep running, UNICEF says.

It also calls for the protection of those who operate and maintain water systems and for all attacks to be systematically documented.
